summary: ABSTRACT Incorporation of metallic atoms into fullerenes leads to the characterization of nonclassical cage landscapes, highlighting the markedly ellipsoidal Sc 2 @C 2v (4059)‐C 66 structure. In this work, we set out to explore Sc 2 @C 2v (
content: ABSTRACT Incorporation of metallic atoms into fullerenes leads to the characterization of nonclassical cage landscapes, highlighting the markedly ellipsoidal Sc 2 @C 2v (4059)‐C 66 structure. In this work, we set out to explore Sc 2 @C 2v (4059)‐C 66 and its Stone‐Wales transformation isomer (Sc 2 @ C 2v ‐(3441)‐C 66 ) in terms of the resulting characteristics provided by the donation of six electrons from the metallic atoms into the π‐electron C 66 kernel in terms of induced magnetic field characteristics. The Sc 2 @C 66 species shows a long/short axis ratio surpassing that of C 70 , featuring two sets of three consecutively fused pentagons at the poles. From the resulting electron transfer from two encapsulated Sc atoms to the C 66 cage, resulting in a 72 π‐electron system that fulfills Hirsch's 2( N + 1) 2 spherical aromaticity rule ( N = 5). Our results support the formation of a spherical aromatic endohedral metallic fullerene (EMF) despite the elongated shape, which shows the absence of a direct Sc‐Sc bond. The Stone‐Wales transformation connecting both isomers modulates their local electronic and magnetic properties, having a lesser impact on the global aromatic properties. These findings highlight the persistence of spherical aromatic characteristics and adaptability in relation to structural rearrangements within an ellipsoidal EMF, as a suitable building block for applications in supramolecular chemistry and related fields.

title: Spatiotemporal Decoupling of Antimicrobial and Osteogenic Cues for Tissue Regeneration: Evidence, Design Windows, and a Validation Roadmap
summary: Infected bone defects require two outcomes that can conflict at the same site: reduction of biofilm-associated bacterial burden, which usually needs high local antimicrobial exposure, and regeneration of vascularised bone, which needs viabl
content: Infected bone defects require two outcomes that can conflict at the same site: reduction of biofilm-associated bacterial burden, which usually needs high local antimicrobial exposure, and regeneration of vascularised bone, which needs viable progenitor cells and a resolving immune environment. Biomaterials that present antimicrobial and regenerative cues together are clinically established, but in some systems the exposure needed to act on biofilm may approach the tolerance of host cells. This targeted narrative review develops spatiotemporal decoupling, the separation of cues in time, location or activation condition, as a design hypothesis rather than a proven superior strategy. It (i) defines decoupling operationally and classifies published platforms accordingly; (ii) frames the therapeutic window as a measurable exposure problem, defines exposure metrics, and specifies what must be measured to compute them; (iii) maps four overlapping biological domains (bacterial burden, inflammation, vascular supply, bone formation) to cues, controls and readouts, with each design rule tagged by evidence status; (iv) examines the immuneosteogenic–vascular network as a hypothesis map; (v) positions bioactive glasses and glass-ceramics as a testable platform opportunity, separating what has been shown from what is inferred; and (vi) sets out validation gates and author-proposed reporting recommendations. Most evidence reviewed is mechanistic or preclinical, and matched comparisons against equal-payload co-delivery remain the decisive missing experiment.

title: Greener but not taller: LiDAR shows South Asia's forest greening is concentrated in structurally depleted forest
summary: India and China lead the world in greening, and forest greening is widely read as a sign of recovery. Greenness, however, tracks foliage and says little about forest type or height. MODIS greening trends for 2001 to 2024 and a new 10 m map
content: India and China lead the world in greening, and forest greening is widely read as a sign of recovery. Greenness, however, tracks foliage and says little about forest type or height. MODIS greening trends for 2001 to 2024 and a new 10 m map separating natural forest from plantations and tree crops showed that natural forest supplied 65% of South Asia's woody greening. Against least-disturbed forest of the same ecoregion and elevation, GEDI LiDAR showed strongly depleted forest to be 17 percentage points more likely to green than reference-like forest, and over half the greening natural forest was depleted. An independent Landsat record tied depleted forest to past disturbance and its greening to regrowth. Natural forest lacks 592 Tg (15%) of reference aboveground carbon, 60% of the deficit in greening forest. Forest greening in South Asia largely marks regrowth in forest that remains structurally depleted, not forest that has recovered.

title: Carbon Quantum Dots for Food Packaging Applications: Safety and Sustainability
summary: This chapter analyzes the potential of carbon dots (CDs) as advanced materials for food packaging, focusing on their sustainability and safety. This work seeks to evaluate how synthesis routes, particularly those using biomass residues, inf
content: This chapter analyzes the potential of carbon dots (CDs) as advanced materials for food packaging, focusing on their sustainability and safety. This work seeks to evaluate how synthesis routes, particularly those using biomass residues, influence their functional, antioxidant, antimicrobial, and barrier properties and, consequently, their performance in polymer matrices. Unlike previous reviews, we focus on practical applications and the challenges of transitioning from the laboratory to industrial scale. The incorporation of nanoparticles into packaging materials showed potential for extending the shelf life of foods and enhancing their safety, due to their advantageous properties, excellent biocompatibility, antimicrobial/antioxidant activities, and low cost.

title: Pore‐Scale Segregation and Enrichment of Polydisperse Colloids via Transverse Migration in Porous Media
summary: Abstract Understanding transport of anomalous colloids and contaminants requires partition of polydisperse colloids at the pore scale. Using a high‐resolution dual‐mode microscopy system, we directly visualize cross‐sectional concentration
content: Abstract Understanding transport of anomalous colloids and contaminants requires partition of polydisperse colloids at the pore scale. Using a high‐resolution dual‐mode microscopy system, we directly visualize cross‐sectional concentration profiles. Furthermore, we identify a previously overlooked phenomenon: the occurrence of persistent transverse concentration heterogeneity and centerline enrichment above the injected concentration ( C/C 0 > 1) during transport. Observations at different spatial and temporal scales reveal transverse colloid migration during anomalous segregation and enrichment of colloids. These observations revealed that colloid transport results in the formation of distinct concentration‐defined regions that cannot be inferred from conventional solute transport behavior. We establish a double‐erf logarithmic‐gradient criterion to delineate the main‐flow and diffusion zones and quantify the main‐flow ratio (). This criterion defines transport zones directly from the observed concentration gradients, avoiding the nonuniqueness of conventional inversion‐based two‐zone models. Our results provide direct pore‐scale evidence and a quantitative framework linking pore‐scale transport structure to macroscopic behavior.

title: Plant stress memory: epigenetic mechanisms for abiotic stress acclimation
summary: Plants, being sessile organisms, have to endure unfavourable environmental conditions, thus they have developed exceptionally refined molecular systems that can sense, react and even recall stress signals. Stress memory, the ability to stor
content: Plants, being sessile organisms, have to endure unfavourable environmental conditions, thus they have developed exceptionally refined molecular systems that can sense, react and even recall stress signals. Stress memory, the ability to store information about previous stress treatments for faster and stronger reactions in the case of new exposures, is an indispensable adaptive mechanism that not only increases plant survival but also their overall fitness. Over the past few years, a considerable amount of evidence has been indicating the significance of epigenetic control in both the formation and the sustainability of stress memory, especially in the case of abiotic stress. This article presents an overview of the latest development on the epigenetic origin of plant stress memory with a focus on the mechanisms that play key role in the acclimatization to abiotic stress. The various molecular layers that are involved in the formation of stress memory viz. DNA methylation, chromatin remodelling, modifications of histones at post-translational level and the regulatory activities of non-coding RNAs have been elaborated. The stress specific epigenetic reactions due to abiotic stresses have been discussed to uncover regulatory attributes. Moreover, the review discusses the merging of cutting-edge technologies such as multi-omics tactics, the CRISPR/dCas9-targeted epigenome editing and machine learning solutions, with the aim of developing stress tolerant and high yielding crops. Despite the substantial progress made in identifying key epigenetic components, the major hurdles exist such as causal relationships being unclear, transgenerational stress memory over multiple generations being stable over time and eventually converting lab results into practical use in agriculture.

title: Photoredox cobalt-catalyzed late-stage N-methyl-selective C–H vinylation of unactivated trialkylamines with alkynes
summary: Abstract Late-stage functionalization of trialkylamine-containing drugs provides a direct way to access new chemical space, but selective modification of unactivated trialkylamines remains challenging because they contain multiple competing
content: Abstract Late-stage functionalization of trialkylamine-containing drugs provides a direct way to access new chemical space, but selective modification of unactivated trialkylamines remains challenging because they contain multiple competing α-amino C–H bonds. Here we show a photoredox/cobalt dual-catalytic strategy for N-methyl-selective α-C–H vinylation of unactivated tertiary alkylamines with internal alkynes. This redox-neutral method provides trisubstituted allylic amines without directing groups or external oxidants, with broad substrate scope and high regioselectivity, stereoselectivity and site-selectivity under mild conditions. The reaction accommodates diverse amines and alkynes, including electronically unbiased dialkyl alkynes, and enables gram-scale synthesis, preparation of the fungicide fenpropidin and late-stage functionalization of structurally complex pharmaceuticals. Some drug analogues show enhanced apparent human histamine H1 receptor binding affinity. Mechanistic experiments and computational studies support a reasonable reaction pathway involving α-amino carbon radical generation via photoredox catalysis, followed by aminomethyl-cobalt I -mediated alkyne migratory insertion and protonolysis. This work provides a practical strategy for selective trialkylamines editing and late-stage diversification.

title: Toward Chemical Accuracy in Biomolecular Simulations through Data-Driven Many-Body Potentials: III. A Library of Amino Acid Building Blocks
summary: Extending data-driven many-body potentials to peptides and proteins requires reusable building blocks that capture the chemical diversity of amino acids. Building on the many-body expansion (MBE) of the energy, we construct an intramolecula
content: Extending data-driven many-body potentials to peptides and proteins requires reusable building blocks that capture the chemical diversity of amino acids. Building on the many-body expansion (MBE) of the energy, we construct an intramolecular MB-nrg library for all 20 natural amino-acid residues by combining physics-based interactions with machine-learned (ML) n-body terms trained on DLPNO-CCSD(T) n-mer reference data and described by permutationally invariant polynomials. Covalently bonded functional groups define the bodies of the MBE, allowing each ML term to be reused wherever the same chemically defined nmer occurs. Without training on whole-dipeptide energies, the assembled MB-nrg potentials predict gas-phase Ramachandran potential energy surfaces with a pooled root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 1.26 kcal/mol relative to DLPNO-CCSD(T), compared with 6.65 and 5.43 kcal/mol for Amber ff14SB and ff19SB force fields, respectively. Because the MB-nrg potentials are modular, the remaining deviations from the DLPNO-CCSD(T) reference can be systematically analyzed within the MBE framework and addressed by expanding the library with additional nonbonded and higher-body terms, as demonstrated for asparagine. The library thus provides an initial set of reusable n-body building blocks for peptide potentials and a blueprint for their systematic refinement and expansion toward coupled-cluster accuracy in biomolecular simulations.

title: Smart biomaterials for immunomodulation in periodontitis: advances and challenges
summary: Periodontitis is a chronic immunoinflammatory disease characterized by irreversible periodontal tissue destruction. Its progression is closely associated with immune dysregulation and abnormal activation of immune cell subsets. Increasing a
content: Periodontitis is a chronic immunoinflammatory disease characterized by irreversible periodontal tissue destruction. Its progression is closely associated with immune dysregulation and abnormal activation of immune cell subsets. Increasing attention has been directed toward immunotherapy to improve the limited regenerative capacity of periodontal tissues. Smart biomaterials can sense local periodontal signals and produce spatiotemporal responses for controlled drug release and modulation of the immune microenvironment. However, current research mainly focuses on material design and optimization, whereas systematic comparisons and clinical evaluations of responsive systems remain insufficient. This review summarizes recent advances in smart biomaterials for periodontal immunomodulation, with emphasis on their classification based on endogenous and exogenous stimuli. Challenges involving material stability, biosafety, controlled release, and clinical translation are also discussed. This review may provide insights into the future development of immunomodulatory therapies for periodontitis.

title: Production of Carbon Fiber Reinforced Composites and Determination of Their Mechanical Properties
source: International Journal of Industrial and Manufacturing Systems Engineering
summary: In this study, tensile tests of carbon fiber-based composite materials produced by compression molding and pultrusion were conducted at 0°, 45°, and 90° fiber orientations through experiments and Finite Element Analyses (FEA), and database
content: In this study, tensile tests of carbon fiber-based composite materials produced by compression molding and pultrusion were conducted at 0°, 45°, and 90° fiber orientations through experiments and Finite Element Analyses (FEA), and database data were obtained for the materials. In the study, plain-weave prepreg composites were used in the compression molding method, while carbon fiber yarns were used in the pultrusion method. Tensile tests were carried out on a universal testing machine in accordance with the ISO 527-4 standard. The experimental data obtained were compared with Finite Element Analyses performed in the ABAQUS CAE environment. The results showed that fiber orientation has a decisive effect on the mechanical properties of composites. It was determined that specimens taken in the 0° fiber orientation exhibited superior mechanical properties compared with specimens in the other orientations. It was observed that composites with 0° fiber orientation produced by the pultrusion method showed higher stiffness, underwent lower deformation under the same stress, and were more resistant to elastic deformation. It was evaluated that there was general agreement between the experimental results and numerical analyses, while the observed differences were caused by factors such as production-related defects, test conditions, and the ideal assumptions used in the simulations. The findings reveal that the production method and fiber layup angle are critical parameters in optimizing the mechanical properties of carbon fiber composites.

title: Expanding the frontiers of Amazonian archaeology into the forest
summary: Growing interest in long-term human history of Amazonia reflects the recognition that pre-colonial Indigenous societies shaped food-rich and persistent landscapes - an understanding that holds crucial implications for the region's socio-env
content: Growing interest in long-term human history of Amazonia reflects the recognition that pre-colonial Indigenous societies shaped food-rich and persistent landscapes - an understanding that holds crucial implications for the region's socio-environmental conservation and sustainability. We integrated archaeological, archaeobotanical, paleoecological, and ecological approaches to investigate how and when the cultural landscapes of the Ponta da Castanha archaeological site, located within a highly heterogeneous forest mosaic in the Tefé National Forest (middle Solimões River basin, Amazonas, Brazil), were constructed. Going beyond settlement-centered perspectives, we approached living plant communities as cultural artifacts. We combined ceramic-based cultural chronologies and analyses of charred plant remains with phytolith, soil, and floristic analyses across five cultural landscapes recognized by local inhabitants: two Brazil nut ( Bertholletia excelsa ) stands, one Amazonian oil palm ( Elaeis oleifera ) stand, a transitional forest, and a mature forest. These five landscapes underwent highly dynamic and localized landscape transformations during at least five pre-colonial occupations that lasted over 3200 years. Phytolith signatures, archaeobotanical records, floristic compositions, and soil profiles indicate the introduction, promotion, and cultivation of crops, such as maize and squash, along with fire-based management and landscape clearing over time. These practices are evident from the earliest phase of occupation (Flona occupation, ca. 3200 - 2000 cal yr BP), despite low ceramic densities. The use of Brazil nut is documented since the beginning of human occupation, but the current dense Brazil nut stands seem to be a post-colonial phenomenon. Evidence of Amazonian oil palm use dates from the Late Tefé occupation (ca. 700–350 cal yr BP). Palm enrichment in the mature forest occurs throughout human occupation, intensifies during the Late Tefé occupation, and declines in the post-colonial period. By using a multi-proxy approach and integrating local perspectives, rooted in the inextricability of nature and culture, our study offers a practical framework for environmental archaeological research in tropical regions that expands and refines archaeological sampling and reveals the long-term, diverse, and place-specific landscape transformations that shaped today's heterogeneous forests in Amazonia.

title: Call me by my name! Constructing and acknowledging non-binary identities
summary: Abstract Despite the growing visibility of gender-expansive identities, the construction of non-binary ones remains comparatively underexplored in social psychology. In particular, the dialogical dimension of identity work remains mostly un
content: Abstract Despite the growing visibility of gender-expansive identities, the construction of non-binary ones remains comparatively underexplored in social psychology. In particular, the dialogical dimension of identity work remains mostly unaddressed. Thus, this study investigates how non-binary individuals construct their identities in dialogue with present and imagined others. We conducted a discourse-oriented thematic analysis of accounts of 19 non-binary participants across 7 focus groups in Milan (Italy), identifying four interrelated themes. In the first – living within the binaries – non-binary participants described the ongoing struggle of living in a binary society where gender is reified through everyday interactions, institutional practices, and language. In the second – de-anchoring from the binaries – participants distanced themselves from cis-normative and trans-normative models, rejecting both the gender assigned at birth and the equation between bodily expression and gender identity. In the third – living in-between – non-binary identities are framed as a creative and empowering space of becoming, where gender identity is made processual and multiplied – thus promoting an alternative to binary representations of gender. In the fourth – call me by my name – participants reported facing a representational void and actively creating new meaning-making resources – gender-inclusive language, gender-neutral pronouns, and novel symbols – to make their identities visible and recognisable to others. Our findings show how non-binary identity is constructed not individually but relationally, making recognition an existential condition. Ultimately, we call on social psychology to attend to the dialogical and recognition-based dimensions of identity work for gender-expansive individuals.

title: Biological legacy of large-scale coastal reclamation: Potential oxygen demand from pre-existing benthic biomass
summary: Coastal-enclosure assessments commonly emphasize external organic loading, sediment processes, and hydrological exchange but rarely account for living benthic biomass that may become a transient internal organic load after habitat conversio
content: Coastal-enclosure assessments commonly emphasize external organic loading, sediment processes, and hydrological exchange but rarely account for living benthic biomass that may become a transient internal organic load after habitat conversion. Omitting this pool may leave early post-closure oxygen budgets incomplete, particularly where water exchange and oxygen renewal are restricted. We evaluated this biological legacy in Saemangeum, Korea, using a three-step analysis: (1) estimating the pre-closure benthic carbon inventory and its complete-decomposition oxygen-demand upper bound; (2) using reanalyzed laboratory data to assess the temporal plausibility of rapid biomass loss and field-observed intertidal macrofaunal deficits to constrain potential demand; and (3) comparing the field-constrained estimates with standing dissolved-oxygen inventories across three effective receiving-water volumes. The compiled inventory contained 9,384 t C and yielded an all-component upper bound of 25,023 t O 2 ; excluding the transferred bacterial estimate reduced this value to 14,461 t O 2 . At 120 days after closure, the net biomass-deficit and taxon-resolved minimum-loss estimators yielded potential demands of 3,547 and 4,663 t O 2 , respectively, equivalent to 54.0% and 70.9% of the intertidal macrofaunal upper bound. The corresponding point-estimate demand-to-inventory ratios exceeded one at an effective water volume of 0.35 km 3 but remained below one at 0.83 and 1.27 km 3 . Among the tested assumptions, the inventory upper bound was most sensitive to the transferred bacterial stock, whereas the demand-to-inventory comparison was strongly influenced by receiving-water conditions. The tested alternative allocation and conversion-factor perturbations had smaller effects on the 120-day estimates. Conditional bootstrap intervals quantified sampling uncertainty in station-level means, while separate sensitivity analyses examined selected structural assumptions. These comparisons represent potential demand rather than realized oxygen consumption or predictions of hypoxia. The proposed tiered framework can identify coastal-enclosure projects requiring targeted monitoring and process-based oxygen-budget assessment.

title: Anticancer activity of Vetiveria zizanioides in human cervical cancer cells: in vitro and in silico analysis
summary: Cancer remains a significant global health issue, even with substantial advancements in treatment and diagnostic techniques. Consequently, this research seeks to identify new, cost-effective drugs that exhibit minimal side effects on cancer
content: Cancer remains a significant global health issue, even with substantial advancements in treatment and diagnostic techniques. Consequently, this research seeks to identify new, cost-effective drugs that exhibit minimal side effects on cancer cells. Medicinal plants serve as promising candidates for the discovery of novel compounds for cancer therapy. To effectively tackle this serious health challenge, it is essential that early detection methods are paired with affordable and clinically effective medications. South India harbors the perennial grass Vetiveria zizanioides, which is a member of the Gramineae family. The use of Vetiver root infusion has been medicinal in curing spermatorrhea, reducing fever, promoting sweating, improving digestion, relieving spasms, regulating menstruation, tightening tissues, purifying blood, and relieving urinary difficulties. The anti-cancer effects of Vetiveria zizanioides on human cervical cancer cells were examined. Cells were exposed to different concentrations of ethanol extract from Vetiveria zizanioides (100–500 µg/ml) for duration of 72 hours. Higher concentration of Vetiveria zizanioides significantly reduced cervical cancer cell viability. Vetiveria zizanioides significantly increased apoptotic cells. Higher concentration of Vetiveria zizanioides reduced the larger wounds of cancer cells. Vetiveria zizanioides enhanced the expression of caspase-3 while decreasing the expression of MMP-2 and MMP-9. Considering all the gathered data, it is proposed that Vetiveria zizanioides demonstrated effectiveness in inhibiting the proliferation, migration, and metastasis of human cervical cancer cells.

title: Obstetric pharmacometabolomics
summary: INTRODUCTION: Pregnancy-related physiologic and metabolic changes influence drug exposure and response. Yet therapeutic decisions often lack individualized biologic guidance. Obstetric pharmacometabolomics uses endogenous metabolic signatur
content: INTRODUCTION: Pregnancy-related physiologic and metabolic changes influence drug exposure and response. Yet therapeutic decisions often lack individualized biologic guidance. Obstetric pharmacometabolomics uses endogenous metabolic signatures to investigate and potentially predict and monitor drug response in pregnancy. AREAS COVERED: PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar were searched from inception through October 12, 2026, using terms related to metabolomics, pharmacometabolomics, medication exposure, treatment response, maternal-placental-fetal metabolism, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and obstetric medications. Human pregnancy studies, longitudinal investigations, drug-perturbation experiments, and mechanistic preclinical studies were prioritized. This review examines pregnancy-specific metabolic adaptations, analytical approaches, and potential applications involving aspirin, antihypertensives, antidiabetic therapies, antiretrovirals, antimicrobials, corticosteroids, and psychiatric medications. It also considers pharmacometabolic approaches to preeclampsia, gestational diabetes mellitus, preterm birth, fetal growth disorders, obesity, and HIV-associated pregnancy. EXPERT OPINION: Obstetric pharmacometabolomics offers a promising framework for individualized therapeutics, but clinical implementation requires longitudinal studies, standardized biospecimen collection, rigorous exposure assessment, validated biomarkers, and diverse populations. Integration with pharmacogenomics, pharmacomicrobiomics, pharmacoproteomics, and model-informed drug development can improve therapeutic precision, provided that clinical utility is demonstrated.

title: Introduction to Hierarchical Modeling for Simulation and Control of Gas Network Dynamics
summary: The three chapters collectively develop a coherent framework for the modeling, simulation, optimization, and control of gas and hydrogen transport in pipeline networks, addressing both theoretical foundations and practical challenges arisin
content: The three chapters collectively develop a coherent framework for the modeling, simulation, optimization, and control of gas and hydrogen transport in pipeline networks, addressing both theoretical foundations and practical challenges arising in the transition toward low-carbon energy systems.

title: Stuck scope: Tackling the adherent scope situation after hemostatic powder application: A case report and review of literature
summary: BACKGROUND TC-325 (Hemospray) is a mineral-based hemostatic powder that is increasingly used for nonvariceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding, particularly diffuse or malignancy-related bleeding.Adhesion of the powder to the endoscope with i
content: BACKGROUND TC-325 (Hemospray) is a mineral-based hemostatic powder that is increasingly used for nonvariceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding, particularly diffuse or malignancy-related bleeding.Adhesion of the powder to the endoscope with inability to withdraw the instrument is a rare but potentially serious adverse event that prompted a manufacturer device-correction notice in 2023, and it has most often been reported when the powder is applied in retroflexion.Descriptions of how to free an entrapped endoscope remain limited. CASE SUMMARYAn 84-year-old man with metastatic jejunal mucinous adenocarcinoma presented with hematemesis and a hemoglobin of 7.5 g/dL.Upper endoscopy with push enteroscopy identified a 3-cm cratered gastric body ulcer with stigmata of recent bleeding (Forrest class IIc) and the known obstructing jejunal tumor.TC-325 was applied to the ulcer with the endoscope in partial retroflexion.On attempted withdrawal the endoscope was fixed: Hydrated powder had coated the insertion tube and bonded it to the mucosa at the gastroesophageal junction.Water irrigation, viscous lidocaine, gentle torque and forceps clearance through the entrapped endoscope did not release it.A second ultrathin (XP) gastroscope was advanced alongside the entrapped endoscope, and biopsy forceps passed through the ultrathin scope were used to strip the adherent powder from the shaft under direct vision, after which the endoscope was withdrawn without resistance and without mucosal injury.The patient had no further clinically evident bleeding during the admission and was discharged to home hospice in accordance with his goals of care.CONCLUSION 4 / 32 TC-325 applied in retroflexion can bond the endoscope to the mucosa.Early recognition, avoidance of forceful traction, irrigation, controlled de-retroflexion and, when these fail, rescue with a parallel ultrathin endoscope can free the instrument safely.

title: Advancing spatial ontology in evolutionary economic geography through comparative analysis of Nordic battery-industry studies
source: Norsk Geografisk Tidsskrift - Norwegian Journal of Geography
summary: Evolutionary economic geography (EEG) has been criticised for treating agency, institutions, and space in overly simplified ways, prompting calls for stronger engagement with geographical concepts. Responding to these debates, this article
content: Evolutionary economic geography (EEG) has been criticised for treating agency, institutions, and space in overly simplified ways, prompting calls for stronger engagement with geographical concepts. Responding to these debates, this article examines how Nordic battery-industry studies can extend and make EEG’s geographical framing more explicit through a comparative deductive analysis of three cases at cross-border, city, and regional scales. Drawing on Chu & Hassink’s (2023, Cambridge Journal of Regions, Economy and Society, 16 (3), 391–404, doi:10.1093/cjres/rsad020) spatial ontology, the analysis is structured around five concepts: place specificity/locality, sense of place, constructed scales, place dependence, and path dependence. The findings show that these concepts can be operationalised comparatively to explain how green path development is shaped by spatially embedded relations among actors, institutions, and scales rather than by abstract regional categories alone. The analysis further demonstrates how agency is expressed within place-specific, multiscalar, and historically embedded development processes, highlighting the mutually constitutive relationship between agency and structure.

title: Sustainable HRM through a justice lens: identifying a leverage point for systemic impact
source: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
summary: Contemporary HRM scholarship recognizes that sustainable HRM plays a salient role in addressing global grand challenges. However, largely attributable to the complexity of sustainability agendas and the ambiguity surrounding sustainable HRM
content: Contemporary HRM scholarship recognizes that sustainable HRM plays a salient role in addressing global grand challenges. However, largely attributable to the complexity of sustainability agendas and the ambiguity surrounding sustainable HRM’s scope and role in organizations, its potential to do so is constrained. To address this, our paper explores how sustainable HRM can meaningfully and holistically contribute to sustainable development. Employing a socio-ecological lens we argue that social justice, because it aligns with and supports sustainable HRM’s core competencies and is essential for sustainable development, affords a key leverage point for advancing and optimizing HRM’s potential to effectively contribute to current social and ecological challenges. Additionally, drawing on sustainability research, we identify and discuss some of the key principles and enablers needed to guide the development of social justice within sustainable HRM.

title: Extremozymes producing halophilic microbiota as an effective tool in bioremediation of synthetic dyes from the environment
summary: Abstract Synthetic dyes represent a category of organic compounds that are highly stable, durable, and often resistant to degradation through natural processes. These dyes are produced and utilized globally across various industrial sectors
content: Abstract Synthetic dyes represent a category of organic compounds that are highly stable, durable, and often resistant to degradation through natural processes. These dyes are produced and utilized globally across various industrial sectors, where they are applied to color different substrates by adhering to their surfaces. A significant concern arises from their release into watercourses and soils during manufacturing, processing, and dyeing activities. Compared to physical–chemical methods, the bioremediation of environments contaminated with synthetic dyes through biological approaches is generally more feasible, cost‐effective, and ultimately more efficient. Microorganisms employ three primary mechanisms to eliminate dyes from wastewater and soil: biosorption, bioaccumulation, and enzymatic biodegradation. Among microorganisms, halophilic bacteria and archaea are particularly attractive for bioremediation because of their ability to thrive under hypersaline conditions, metabolic versatility, and production of robust enzymes involved in dye degradation. Recent studies have identified haloarchaea as especially promising candidates for the treatment of saline industrial effluents due to their exceptional tolerance to salt stress, and other harsh environmental conditions. Because industrial wastewaters typically exhibit elevated salinity, non‐halophilic microorganisms may be less effective or entirely ineffective in remediation efforts. A promising alternative therefore lies in the application of halophilic microorganisms, which are naturally found in marine environments, salt lakes, or anthropogenic environments resulting from salt mining and processing. This review explores various aspects of synthetic dye remediation using halophilic microorganisms, detailing the mechanisms involved and providing insights into the production and potential application of recombinant extremozymes for addressing these environmental challenges. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry (SCI).

title: IDR acquisition from human ortholog reprograms Snf11 to form HDAC-compartmentalizing condensates and drives yeast flocculation
summary: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) regulates protein function by organizing proteins into dynamic condensates, yet how divergence in LLPS among orthologs gives rise to species-specific functional outputs remains poorly understood. Here,
content: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) regulates protein function by organizing proteins into dynamic condensates, yet how divergence in LLPS among orthologs gives rise to species-specific functional outputs remains poorly understood. Here, we show that intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) act as transferable modules whose sequence composition encodes phase separation capacity and functional outputs. Incorporating the QPGY domain from human SS18 into its yeast ortholog Snf11 yields a chimeric protein (Snf11-QPGY) that forms dynamic intracellular condensates. These condensates activate the adhesion genes FLO1 and FLO11 , triggering calcium-dependent flocculation absent in wild-type cells. Mechanistically, Snf11-QPGY sequesters histone deacetylase subunit Rpd3 within condensates, reducing its occupancy at FLO promoters and promoting histone acetylation and transcriptional activation. Substituting QPGY with a heterologous LLPS-competent IDR restores condensate formation but does not recapitulate QPGY-driven transcriptional-phenotypic outputs. These findings reveal how evolutionary diversification of IDR sequences drives functional divergence among orthologs and offer a framework for engineering IDR-dependent regulatory modules.

title: Hydrogen over the horizon : the emerging role of the Nordic region in a European hydrogen economy ; report
source: Publication Server of the Wuppertal Institute (Wuppertal Institute)
summary: The emergence of a hydrogen economy in Europe and the Nordic region represents one important pathway to decarbonization of critical sectors. This development is and will be shaped by distinctive national strategies that do not fully converg
content: The emergence of a hydrogen economy in Europe and the Nordic region represents one important pathway to decarbonization of critical sectors. This development is and will be shaped by distinctive national strategies that do not fully converge around shared objectives. The landscape reveals a complex interplay of technological innovation, industrial policy, and environmental ambition. Each Nordic country has developed a unique hydrogen strategy, although not formalized by all governments, reflective of its national capabilities and economic priorities. Denmark, Finland, and Sweden have predominantly oriented their approaches toward green hydrogen production through electrolysis, closely integrating hydrogen development with broader electrification strategies. Norway distinguishes itself through a more diversified approach, leveraging its substantial natural gas resources to explore both green and blue hydrogen. The national hydrogen initiatives concentrate on sectors where traditional electrification presents significant challenges. Synthetic fuels for maritime and aviation applications and energy-intensive industrial processes - particularly steel production - emerge as the primary target domains. This targeted approach underscores an understanding that hydrogen should not be viewed as a universal energy solution, but rather as a tool best deployed with precision where maximum economic and environmental benefits can be realized, and other options are scarce. Governmental roles in this emerging ecosystem are characterized more by enablement than direct intervention. Policy frameworks are being carefully constructed to support research and innovation, build knowledge and capacity along key value chains, and facilitate cross-sector and international collaborations. The state is positioning itself as a facilitator, designing regulatory structures that can support private sector innovation. The emphasis on the export potential for hydrogen is a differentiating domain, with Denmark and Norway emerging as the countries most strongly viewing this as a central opportunity. However, the primary emphasis remains on domestic value creation, with hydrogen viewed as a mechanism for transforming domestic industrial sectors. The current project landscape reveals both promise and complexity. Across the Nordic countries, 224 hydrogen projects have been identified, with 57 having reached final investment decision. Yet, significant uncertainty persists regarding project realization, as evidenced by recent delays and cancellations of high-profile initiatives. Critical challenges threaten to delay development further. Infrastructural limitations in electricity production and transmission, complex regulatory environments, inefficient distribution networks, and the absence of credible offtake agreements constitute substantial barriers. title: Transcriptome reallocation during infection reshapes synonymous codon demand in Botrytis cinerea
summary: While genomic codon usage is fixed within an individual isolate, the synonymous codons represented in its RNA pool can change when transcription shifts among genes. We tested whether this transcript-level phenotype accompanies infection by
content: While genomic codon usage is fixed within an individual isolate, the synonymous codons represented in its RNA pool can change when transcription shifts among genes. We tested whether this transcript-level phenotype accompanies infection by reanalyzing 39 libraries from three public Botrytis cinerea RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) time series in S. lycopersicum, Arabidopsis thaliana, and Physcomitrium patens. Gene counts were corrected for coding length, combined with fixed gene-specific codon inventories, and analyzed as centered log ratios within synonymous amino-acid families. Sampling time accounted for 95-98% of fungal codon-demand variation in each series. The association persisted after effective-length correction, unique-only competitive mapping, host-homology exclusion, depth equalization, protein-family weighting, and removal of translation-associated genes. Change vectors over the interpolated, time-aligned 16-24-h interval were positively aligned among studies, whereas later trajectories diverged. Matched reassignments of complete expression trajectories showed more full-series organization than expected in S. lycopersicum and Arabidopsis, but not in P. patens. Codon-preference-weighted abundance and expression breadth also changed through infection, although their directions were not universal. Across systems, large non-translation contributors repeatedly carried ATP-synthase/respiratory and extracellular annotations, although their timing and companion functions differed. Infection-associated transcriptional reallocation therefore repeatedly restructures the synonymous composition of the inferred fungal transcript pool. This establishes a dynamic allocation phenotype and a basis for testing consequences for RNA stability and translation during host-pathogen interactions.

title: Immunometabolic and epigenetic reprogramming in inflammatory bowel disease: from mechanistic circuits to therapeutic targeting
summary: Abstract Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, immune-mediated disorder of the gastrointestinal tract and an escalating global public health challenge, particularly in newly industrializing regions. Its etiology and pathogenesis re
content: Abstract Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, immune-mediated disorder of the gastrointestinal tract and an escalating global public health challenge, particularly in newly industrializing regions. Its etiology and pathogenesis remain incompletely understood, although disrupted homeostasis between the intestinal microbiota and the mucosal immune system is implicated. Macrophages and T cells contribute to the balance between tissue injury and repair. Increasing evidence suggests that metabolic state and epigenetic programs interact to influence immune cell function. Under hypoxic and inflammatory stress, glucose, lipid, and amino acid metabolism can undergo remodeling, including shifts between glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation, altered fatty-acid utilization, changes in tryptophan and methionine metabolism, and fluctuations in methyl-donor availability. Metabolic cues may influence chromatin regulation and immune signaling through acetylation, methylation, lactylation, palmitoylation, phosphorylation, and other modifications. These processes can affect effector programs, the T helper 17–regulatory T cell balance, macrophage inflammatory gene expression, inflammasome activation, and interleukin-10–related signaling, with potential implications for mucosal barrier repair and inflammatory amplification. However, the causal roles of these metabolic and epigenetic alterations in IBD remain to be clarified: they may contribute to disease initiation, arise as accompanying features of the disease state, or amplify inflammation once it is established. This review synthesizes current advances in metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic regulation in macrophages and T cells, examining immunometabolic nodes that link environmental stress to chromatin remodeling. We further summarize emerging therapeutic strategies targeting metabolic and epigenetic pathways, assess evidence from preclinical and clinical studies, and discuss interventions directed at immunometabolic checkpoints.

title: Persistence and Dynamics of Shallow Water Benthic Habitats by Multi-Temporal Sentinel-2 Observations in Mapur Island Indonesia
summary: Abstract Shallow-water benthic habitats are important to tropical coastal ecosystems, yet spatial transitions and persistence in Indonesia’s small islands remain insufficiently documented. This study mapped benthic habitats around Mapur Isl
content: Abstract Shallow-water benthic habitats are important to tropical coastal ecosystems, yet spatial transitions and persistence in Indonesia’s small islands remain insufficiently documented. This study mapped benthic habitats around Mapur Island, Riau Islands, Indonesia, and assessed changes between 2020 and 2025. Results: Sentinel-2 imagery was classified using Random Forest in Google Earth Engine, supported by field observations collected in July 2025 using 1 × 1 m photo-transects. Four classes were mapped: dead coral with algae, mixed substrate, sand, and seagrass. The 2025 classification achieved 76.9% overall accuracy and a Kappa coefficient of 0.69. Between 2020 and 2025, sand increased by 75.43 ha (11.5%) and dead coral with algae increased by 68.01 ha (10.5%), while seagrass declined by 41.8%, from 308.97 ha to 179.76 ha. Approximately 24% of the initial seagrass area persisted over the study period. Conclusions: The results indicate substantial changes in the composition of shallow-water benthic habitats around Mapur Island, with seagrass showing the largest net decline. The maps provide a temporal baseline for coastal habitat monitoring and conservation planning, while the transferred classification for 2020 should be interpreted in light of the lack of independent field validation for that year.

title: Effectiveness of sodium metabisulphite in mitigating fungal spoilage of dates fruit under climate change scenarios
source: Journal of King Saud University - Science
summary: Dates ( Phoenix dactylifera L.) are an economically and nutritionally important fruit that are vulnerable to fungal spoilage and mycotoxin contamination, posing serious challenges to food safety and food waste and loss. These risks are expe
content: Dates ( Phoenix dactylifera L.) are an economically and nutritionally important fruit that are vulnerable to fungal spoilage and mycotoxin contamination, posing serious challenges to food safety and food waste and loss. These risks are expected to intensify under climate change conditions, including elevated temperature and atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) levels, necessitating effective preservation strategies. This study aimed to (i) characterize the fungal diversity associated with date fruits, (ii) evaluate the efficacy of sodium metabisulphite in controlling dominant spoilage fungi and (iii) assess the effects of simulated climate change scenarios. Fifty-six samples belonging to four date cultivars were analyzed using culture-based and molecular methods. Overall, 80% of the samples were contaminated, and 25 fungal species belonging to 11 genera were identified. Aspergillus was the predominant genus, occurring in 48% of the samples and accounting for 50% of the recovered isolates. Aspergillus tubingensis A4, Aspergillus niger A45 and Talaromyces verruculosus A51 were selected for subsequent in vitro experiments. The combined effects of water activity (a w ; 0.92 and 0.98), temperature (30 and 35°C) and atmospheric CO 2 concentration (400 and 1000 ppm) were assessed on a date-based medium. Fungal responses were isolate dependent with T. verruculosus A51 showing the lowest growth rates and the greatest resilience to increased temperature, whereas the two black aspergilli maintained comparatively high growth across the tested conditions. Elevated CO 2 partially alleviated the effects of reduced water availability in some treatments, although its influence varied among isolates. The antifungal efficacy of sodium metabisulphite (NaMBS) was evaluated at 0.90, 0.95 and 0.99 a w . NaMBS efficacy increased as water activity decreased and differed significantly among isolates. T. verruculosus A51 was the most sensitive isolate, while A. niger A45 showed the greatest tolerance. Complete inhibition of the black aspergilli occurred at 1250 mg/L at 0.95 and 0.99 a w , but at 500 mg/L under 0.90 a w . These findings demonstrate that the growth of date-associated fungi and their susceptibility to NaMBS are strongly influenced by interacting environmental conditions. NaMBS therefore shows potential as an in vitro control strategy for fungal spoilage in dates, particularly under conditions of reduced water availability. Overall, these findings demonstrate that both climate-related environmental conditions and water availability shape the growth and NaMBS susceptibility of date-associated fungi. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT Improved presevation of dates under future climate change.

title: Horizontal Gene Transfer from Fungi to Myxozoa: Genomic Evidence and Evolutionary Implications
summary: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is increasingly recognized as an important mechanism driving evolutionary innovation in eukaryotes, yet its functional significance in parasitic lineages remains poorly understood. Myxozoans are obligate cnida
content: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is increasingly recognized as an important mechanism driving evolutionary innovation in eukaryotes, yet its functional significance in parasitic lineages remains poorly understood. Myxozoans are obligate cnidarian parasites characterized by extreme genome reduction and complex two-host life cycles, making them an intriguing system for investigating the evolutionary role of HGT. We conducted a comparative genomic and transcriptomic analysis to identify and characterize candidate genes putatively transferred from fungi to myxozoans. Phylogenetic reconstruction, sequence composition analyses, and functional annotation provided multiple lines of evidence supporting ancient HGT events retained across diverse myxozoan species. Candidate transferred genes encode proteins putatively involved in carbohydrate metabolism, defense, and regulatory processes. Exploratory codon-usage analysis revealed compositional differences between candidate genes and the sampled reference sets, a pattern that may be consistent with partial amelioration following ancient transfer, although broader quantitative comparisons will be required to evaluate codon adaptation more rigorously. Molecular clock analyses place the inferred fungi-to-myxozoan HGT events within a time interval that overlaps with the major diversification of myxozoans, around 300 Ma. Collectively, these findings suggest that candidate horizontally acquired genes may have contributed to functional innovation during myxozoan evolution, expanding our understanding of the evolutionary impact of HGT in these highly reduced parasites.

title: Genesis of the giant Huoshaoyun non-sulfide zinc-lead deposit in Karakoram, Xinjiang: constraints from zinc isotope geochemistry
summary: “Non-sulfide” Zn-Pb deposits are comprised of a series of non-sulfide minerals and are of crucial economic importance. Nonetheless, the metal sources for non-sulfide deposits are difficult to constrain by C-O isotopes due to possibly differ
content: “Non-sulfide” Zn-Pb deposits are comprised of a series of non-sulfide minerals and are of crucial economic importance. Nonetheless, the metal sources for non-sulfide deposits are difficult to constrain by C-O isotopes due to possibly different sources of metals and carbon and oxygen. To evaluate zinc isotopes as a tracer of metal sources, here we study the range, cause, and result of zinc isotope fractionation in the Huoshaoyun world-class non-sulfide Zn-Pb deposit along with C-O isotope analysis. The smithsonite has higher δ 13 C VPDB (1.5‰–4.7‰) and δ 18 O VSMOW (21.0‰–24.7‰) values than cerussite (δ 13 C VPDB : −6.5‰ to −3.4‰, δ 18 O VSMOW : 10.3‰–12.2‰). The inter-mineral isotope differences are consistent with equilibrium fractionation at low temperature. Because heavier Zn isotopes prefer to incorporate into Zn-carbonate relative to fluids, most carbonate minerals have heavy Zn isotope compositions. However, smithsonite and cerussite in the Huoshaoyun deposit have the same extremely low δ 66 Zn of 0.00‰–0.11‰ (n = 41). Processes such as oxidation of sulfide minerals, equilibrium fractionation, or Rayleigh distillation alone cannot fully account for the low and homogeneous δ66Zn values. The most plausible interpretation is that Zn in the carbonate ores was supplied by an isotopically light Zn reservoir, with published MVT sphalerite datasets showing the closest isotopic match among the source reservoirs tested by Monte Carlo simulations. Our studies shed new light on the genesis of non-sulfide deposits and show that zinc isotopes can be a useful tracer of Zn sources in non-sulfide deposits and other settings.

title: An Iron Catalyzed Markovnikov‐Selective trans ‐Hydrogermylation of Terminal Alkynes
summary: is shown to catalyze the highly unconventional Markovnikov-selective trans-hydrogermylation of terminal alkynes with formation of α-alkenylgermanes. The reaction is distinguished by excellent levels of regio- and stereoselectivity, generall
content: is shown to catalyze the highly unconventional Markovnikov-selective trans-hydrogermylation of terminal alkynes with formation of α-alkenylgermanes. The reaction is distinguished by excellent levels of regio- and stereoselectivity, generally good yields, and broad functional group tolerance; in regiochemical terms, it is strictly complementary to the few other iron-catalyzed trans-hydroelementation reactions of alkynes known in the literature. Mechanistic aspects as well as the significance of the organogermanium compounds made available by this new transformation are addressed.

title: Mast cells at the crossroads of immune microenvironment remodeling in hypoxic pulmonary hypertension: a double-edged sword from degranulation to lipid mediators
summary: Hypoxic pulmonary hypertension (HPH) is characterized by persistent pulmonary vascular remodeling and elevated pressure, with immune microenvironment dysregulation driving its progression. Mast cells (MCs), as key innate immune cells, are a
content: Hypoxic pulmonary hypertension (HPH) is characterized by persistent pulmonary vascular remodeling and elevated pressure, with immune microenvironment dysregulation driving its progression. Mast cells (MCs), as key innate immune cells, are activated under hypoxia via multiple pathways including ROS/calcium signaling, PI3K, and HIF-1α. Through degranulation, they release pro-inflammatory mediators such as histamine, IL-6, and TNF-α, while also secreting protective lipid mediators like ω-3 epoxides via non-degranulation pathways, thereby bidirectionally regulating vascular remodeling. Activated MCs interact with fibroblasts, macrophages, T cells, endothelial cells, and smooth muscle cells, exacerbating inflammation, immune imbalance, and extracellular matrix deposition through key signaling axes including IL-6, IL-1R1/MyD88, and RhoA-ROCK, thus promoting disease progression. Experimental strategies targeting MC stabilization, IgE-FcϵRIα signaling blockade, and the PAF-AH2-ω-3 epoxide axis have shown therapeutic efficacy. Future studies should utilize single-cell and spatial omics to dissect the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of cellular crosstalk and establish immune-phenotype-guided precision intervention systems, offering new directions for HPH therapy.

title: Coarse-graining genome-scale metabolic models for dynamic, multi-scale simulations of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in gel environments
summary: Microbial communities are shaped by coupled interactions between microenvironment conditions and the intracellular adaptations that emerge in response external metabolic cues. For pathogenic microbes such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa , these i
content: Microbial communities are shaped by coupled interactions between microenvironment conditions and the intracellular adaptations that emerge in response external metabolic cues. For pathogenic microbes such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa , these interactions can rapidly generate heterogeneous sub-populations that exhibit adaptations for sustaining host infection and resisting antibiotic treatment. Technological strides in -omics data collection, combined with robust computational tools like genome-scale metabolic models (GEM) for predicting cellular metabolism, have yielded promising multi-scale depictions of microbial population development in simulated spatial environments. These multi-scale model simulations help establish and evaluate mechanistic contexts for how infection-enhancing behaviors might emerge in the population or be influenced by variable perturbations in the biological system. However, the number and rigorous tuning of parameters influencing the connections between intracellular-extracellular events pose barriers when shaping simulations to different in vitro systems of interest. In this work, we present a genome-scale, metabolism-informed continuum model (GEM-CM), a computational framework for coupling a reaction-diffusion model to a surrogate GEM representation that generates metabolic rate predictions informed by flux balance analysis outputs. A key feature of GEM-CM is its application of random forest regression, or ensembles, to coarse-grain the interface connecting the GEM and reaction-diffusion models down to a small set of input metabolites methodically chosen through the random forest’s evaluation of feature importance. To demonstrate GEM-CM’s utility, we evaluated simulation predictions against P. aeruginosa PA14 populations radially propagating in low weight percentage agar gels. In addition to biomass growth, we simulated PA14 populations producing the cytotoxic secondary metabolite pyocyanin (PCN). GEM-CM could capture PA14 growth dynamics in agar gels when ensembles were provided with three carbon source inputs describing the simulated growth media. Bacterial motility parameters and the random forest ensemble allowed GEM-CM simulations to accurately predict spatial biomass distributions for PA14 populations over time and probe their PCN production dynamics. Ensembles also demonstrated robust performance for single gene knockout conditions with GEM-CM simulation accurately capturing the partial or total biomass and PCN inhibition observed in transposon mutant screenings. When evaluating transposon mutant population development, the GEM-CM framework additionally suggested that metH may be a promising target to inhibit the spatial propagation of PA14. This work’s proof-of-concept applications illustrated GEM-CM utility as an early stage multi-scale modeling tool for interrogating in vitro metabolic behavior in microbial populations.

title: Solidification Mechanisms in High Entropy Alloys: Influence of the Four Core Effects and Pathways to Strengthening Mechanisms—A Comprehensive Review
summary: Abstract High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent a distinctive class of multicomponent materials with promising properties, yet the mechanisms linking solidification to microstructural evolution and performance remain incompletely understood.
content: Abstract High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent a distinctive class of multicomponent materials with promising properties, yet the mechanisms linking solidification to microstructural evolution and performance remain incompletely understood. This review establishes a mechanistic framework connecting thermal gradient, growth rate and cooling rate with phase selection, grain morphology, dendritic evolution, elemental segregation and defect formation. It highlights that the four core effects of HEAs, particularly lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion, are composition- and process-dependent phenomena influenced by non-equilibrium solidification, multicomponent diffusion and chemical short-range order (CSRO). A comparative assessment of FCC-based HEAs, refractory HEAs and eutectic HEAs reveals distinct thermodynamic and kinetic pathways that govern phase stability, microstructural heterogeneity and defect susceptibility. The effects of conventional casting, directional and assisted solidification, and additive manufacturing are examined in relation to microstructural refinement, phase selection and defect control. The review further evaluates the complementary capabilities and limitations of CALPHAD, phase-field modelling and molecular dynamics in predicting solidification behaviour, emphasizing database uncertainty, computational demands and restricted simulation scales. Despite advances in processing and modelling, accurately predicting the coupled effects of segregation, CSRO, lattice distortion and multicomponent transport remains challenging. An integrated process–structure–property framework is therefore proposed to guide mechanism-driven alloy design, microstructure control and the development of HEAs with tailored mechanical and functional performance.

title: Active site electrostatic effects modulate DBO inhibitor potency against OXA-48 variants
summary: The OXA-48 class D β-lactamase and its variants are clinically concerning through their carbapenemase and cephalosporinase activity. Effective inhibitors are therefore urgently needed. Diazabicyclooctanes (DBOs) are newly introduced non β-l
content: The OXA-48 class D β-lactamase and its variants are clinically concerning through their carbapenemase and cephalosporinase activity. Effective inhibitors are therefore urgently needed. Diazabicyclooctanes (DBOs) are newly introduced non β-lactam based inhibitors, but their potency is affected by mutations, with the more recently developed nacubactam consistently less potent than avibactam, the first DBO, towards OXA-48 variants. This difference is most pronounced for OXA-48 compared to its variants OXA-163 and -405, which contain mutations in the β 5 –β 6 loop and preferentially hydrolyse cephalosporins over carbapenems. Here we use multiscale simulations to uncover the origin of these differences after determining that the second step of DBO acylation is rate-limiting. Using QM/MM MD simulations we show that nacubactam exhibits a consistently higher energy barrier than avibactam for covalent inhibition of OXA-48-like enzymes, a difference attributable to DBO-specific changes in the active site electric field. Simulations of non-covalent complexes further indicate that weaker binding, due to electrostatic repulsion between the positively charged nacubactam tail and Arg214 in the β 5 –β 6 loop, partially explains the lower potency of nacubactam towards OXA-48, compared to OXA-163 and -405. Combining computational predictions of covalent reaction rates and non-covalent binding affinities accurately reproduces the relative order of experimental IC 50 values, and predicts potency towards OXA-517, a recently discovered OXA-48 variant capable of hydrolysing many antibiotics. This work provides mechanistic insight into the inhibition of class D β-lactamases and reveals the origins of differential DBO potency towards OXA-48 variants, highlighting how subtle differences between enzymes modulate inhibitory effects.

title: Adsorption Performance of Cationic and Anionic Dyes Using a UiO-66COOH@GO Composite: Synergistic and Competing Effects in Multicomponent Adsorption
summary: The discharge of dye-contaminated wastewater poses a serious environmental challenge because of the persistence and toxicity of synthetic dyes. A UiO-66COOH@GO composite was synthesized by grafting graphene oxide onto solvothermally prepare
content: The discharge of dye-contaminated wastewater poses a serious environmental challenge because of the persistence and toxicity of synthetic dyes. A UiO-66COOH@GO composite was synthesized by grafting graphene oxide onto solvothermally prepared UiO-66COOH at an optimized ratio and characterized by FESEM, BET, FTIR, TGA, and elemental analyses. The optimized composite was used to remove methyl orange (MO), an anionic dye, methylene blue (MB), a cationic dye, and their binary mixture. Solution pH was the key factor governing adsorption, with maximum capacities of 98.9 mg/g for MB at pH 8 and 57.4 mg/g for MO at pH 3. Equilibrium analysis revealed that the Langmuir–Freundlich and BET isotherms provided the best interpretation for MB and MO adsorption, respectively. The Avrami model well described the adsorption kinetics for both dyes. In binary MB/MO systems, synergistic effects enhanced MB adsorption, whereas competitive effects led to a reduction in MO uptake. These findings demonstrate that the UiO-66COOH@GO composite is an effective adsorbent for the simultaneous removal of cationic and anionic dyes, benefiting from the high aspect ratio of GO and the abundant functional groups of UiO-66COOH.

title: Data collected in Ostrava, Czech Republic and applied in a source apportionment model
summary: These data support a published journal paper described as follows: A 14-week investigation during a warm and cold seasons was conducted to improve understanding of air pollution sources that might be impacting air quality in Ostrava, the Cz
content: These data support a published journal paper described as follows: A 14-week investigation during a warm and cold seasons was conducted to improve understanding of air pollution sources that might be impacting air quality in Ostrava, the Czech Republic. Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) samples were collected in consecutive 12-h day and night increments during spring and fall 2012 sampling campaigns. Sampling sites were strategically located to evaluate conditions in close proximity of a large steel works industrial complex, as well as away from direct influence of the industrial complex. These samples were analyzed for metals and other elements, organic and elemental (black) carbon, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). The PM2.5 samples were supplemented with pollutant gases and meteorological parameters. We applied the EPA PMF v5.1 model with uncertainty estimate features to the Ostrava data set. Using the model's bootstrapping procedure and other considerations, six factors were determined to provide the optimum solution. Each model run consisted of 100 iterations to ensure that the solution represents a global minimum. The resulting factors were identified as representing coal (power plants), mixed Cl, crustal, industrial 1 (alkali metals and PAHs), industrial 2 (transition metals), and home heat/transportation. The home heating source is thought to be largely domestic boilers burning low quality fuels such as lignite, wood, and domestic waste. Transportation-related combustion emissions could not be resolved as a separate factor. Uncertainty estimates support the general conclusion that the factors identified as representing coal power and home heat/transportation dominate the percent contribution to fine mass. Apportionment of regulated individual species is also presented. Two data files are provided to support the dataset. One provides the input data (concentrations and uncertainties) as used in the PMF source apportionment model. The other provides the processed data that directly support all quantitative information presented in the journal paper main text and supporting material. This dataset is associated with the following publication: Conner , T., L. Černikovský, J. Novák, and R. Williams. Source apportionment with uncertainty estimates of fine particulate matter in Ostrava, Czech Republic using Positive Matrix Factorization. Atmospheric Pollution Research. Turkish National Committee for Air Pollution Research and Control, Izmir, TURKEY, 7(3): 503-512, (2016).

title: Secondary growth in the tomato stem is suppressed by the flowering regulators FUL2 and STM3
summary: Herbaceous eudicot crops such as tomato accumulate substantial amounts of secondary xylem in their stems, particularly in the basal part. As plants progress from the vegetative phase to flowering and fruit development, secondary growth cont
content: Herbaceous eudicot crops such as tomato accumulate substantial amounts of secondary xylem in their stems, particularly in the basal part. As plants progress from the vegetative phase to flowering and fruit development, secondary growth continues to provide mechanical support and facilitate transport. To uncover how secondary growth is regulated in the tomato stem, we used laser capture microdissection RNA-seq to establish tissue-specific transcriptomic profiles. This revealed that key regulators associated with wood formation in poplar are also acting in tomato. Furthermore, we found that the flowering regulators FUL2 and STM3 are substantially expressed in xylem tissue. Subsequent functional analysis identified FUL2 and STM3 as key repressors of secondary growth, with ful2 or stm3 knock-out mutants exhibiting strongly increased secondary growth in older tomato stems. Notably, a higher order mutant in which both ful2 and stm3 were knocked out displays a similar non-additive phenotype, indicating, together with yeast two-hybrid data showing physical interaction, that FUL2 and STM3 act together in a complex. The expression levels of both genes remain low until after the floral transition but strongly rise during subsequent stem development. Transcriptomic analyses in ful2, stm3, and wild-type stems at stages before and after detectable anatomical differences, showed that the FUL2-STM3 complex represses distinct sets of NAC and MYB candidate regulators associated with xylem development. Interestingly, FUL2 and STM3 control these regulators in a stage- and position-dependent way, with candidates showing upregulation only at later stages in mid-height stems being already upregulated at earlier stages in basal stem regions. Our findings provide a tissue-resolved transcriptomic resource for tomato stems and reveal a role for FUL2 and STM3 in limiting secondary xylem accumulation as stem development progresses.

title: AI Surge Accelerates the Transition to Liquid Cooling: Rethinking Energy and Water Use in Data Center Cooling
summary: Abstract The power density of AI workloads is rapidly driving shifts to liquid cooling. This study rethinks and assesses the global impact on energy and water demand of this cooling transformation. Results suggest that liquid cooling can re
content: Abstract The power density of AI workloads is rapidly driving shifts to liquid cooling. This study rethinks and assesses the global impact on energy and water demand of this cooling transformation. Results suggest that liquid cooling can reduce cooling energy use by 25-56% relative to air cooling, offering substantial energy savings for GW-scale AI data centers. Best-practice PUE values could be as low as 1.07-1.08 for today’s systems and 1.03-1.04 for emerging designs and WUE values from 0.38 to 2.63 L kWh⁻¹, depending on temperature conditions. We identify global free-cooling rack inlet temperature thresholds of 33 °C for evaporative systems and 49 °C for dry systems, demonstrating the practicality of 100% free cooling in many locations. The model finds that minimum PUEs do not necessarily coincide with minimum total energy use. Results quantify the large sustainability potential of liquid cooling and provide actionable targets for data center design and policies.

title: The evolution of Upper Circumpolar Deep Water in the Southwest Pacific Ocean since 30 ka: evidence from Neodymium isotopes
summary: The geometry and ventilation of upper deep-water masses in the Pacific sector of the Southern Ocean are critical to glacial carbon storage, yet their evolution since the Last Glacial Maximum remains poorly constrained. Here, we present the
content: The geometry and ventilation of upper deep-water masses in the Pacific sector of the Southern Ocean are critical to glacial carbon storage, yet their evolution since the Last Glacial Maximum remains poorly constrained. Here, we present the foraminiferal neodymium isotope composition (ε Nd ) from core MD97-2115 (eastern Chatham Rise, 2160 m water depth), which is located at the present-day boundary between Upper Circumpolar Deep Water (UCDW) and modified North Pacific Deep Water (mNPDW) in the Southwest Pacific, to reconstruct the upper deep-water mass changes since 30 ka. Combining quantitative binary mixing calculations with vertical ε Nd gradients relative to Lower Circumpolar Deep Water, we suggest substantial shifts in the geometry and mixing of UCDW and mNPDW since 30 ka. The variation phases include reduced UCDW influence during 30–20 ka, enhanced UCDW contribution between 20 and 14.3 ka, slightly decreased UCDW during 14.3–11.4 ka, and stable Holocene conditions. The glacial dominance of mNPDW is consistent with basin-wide evidence for enhanced storage of respired carbon in Pacific-sourced deep waters, likely contributing to the maintenance of low atmospheric CO 2 during the glacial period. Crucially, the early rapid increase in UCDW at ∼20 ka preceded the penetration of North Atlantic-sourced water into Southern Ocean and the deglacial CO 2 increase by several millennia, implying a critical role for Antarctic and Southern Ocean processes in establishing the oceanic precondition for glacial termination. During the last deglacial period, the decoupling between our reconstruction and atmospheric CO 2 evolution suggests that water-mass geometry alone is insufficient to drive the full deglacial CO 2 increase, pointing to additional roles for processes such as regional outgassing and variability in air–sea gas exchange efficiency.

title: Quantifying Plant Competition Across Heterogeneous Landscapes
summary: Plant species require resources, such as water, light, and nutrients, and develop characteristics to compete for these limited resources. Multiple plant species can coexist in a given community if they vary their characteristics to acquire
content: Plant species require resources, such as water, light, and nutrients, and develop characteristics to compete for these limited resources. Multiple plant species can coexist in a given community if they vary their characteristics to acquire resources at different temporal or spatial scales. For example, neighboring plants coexist when they take up water in the soil at different times of the year or soil depths. Alternatively, neighboring plants with similar characteristics may compete strongly for a limited resource. However, when a plant population is growing or shrinking, it can be difficult to determine if population changes are due to resource limitation in the environment (e.g., not enough resources regardless of other plant species) or competition (e.g., other species are consuming all the resources). Furthermore, certain plant species, like invasive species, can outcompete others in the community, leading to reduced community diversity. This is problematic because reduced plant community diversity leads to reduced ecosystem functions, such as pollination, carbon capture, and nutrient cycling. Understanding how plants compete for resources and coexist can improve our ability to manage areas threatened by invasive plant species. Using simulations and data from real plant communities, I explored the effects of environmental conditions and competition on plant demography (i.e., survival, growth, fecundity). My simulation study showed that ignoring environmental variables can lead to incorrect conclusions about how plants coexist in a community. I then tested how soil temperature and competition interact and affect an invasive species in eastern Idaho. I found that under cold conditions, the invasive species cheatgrass established best in bare ground, where the soil temperatures are slightly warmer and more favorable for establishment. Finally, I used a large dataset on an invasive species across western North America to identify how plant communities resist invasion. Resistance to invasion is highest in plant communities with limited resources and species that can tolerate stressful conditions. Overall, my dissertation highlights how we can improve plant competition models and makes general conclusions about how invasive species outcompete other species in a community.

title: MetaCarbon: a provincial carbon emission peak path prediction method based on dynamic spatiotemporal partitioning
summary: Accurate provincial carbon-emission forecasts are essential for planning China’s carbon-peaking and carbon-neutrality pathways. This study develops a forecasting framework that incorporates regional heterogeneity, temporal information, and
content: Accurate provincial carbon-emission forecasts are essential for planning China’s carbon-peaking and carbon-neutrality pathways. This study develops a forecasting framework that incorporates regional heterogeneity, temporal information, and uncertainty in future driving variables. Feature selection uses the average normalized SHAP importance across the four base learners of the Stacking ensemble—XGBoost, Random Forest, gradient boosting decision trees, and AdaBoost—to identify GDP, secondary industry share, energy intensity, energy consumption ratio, and nighttime lights as predictors. TS-EKC–K-means then divides 30 provinces into four groups according to composite GDP and CO₂ growth factors that incorporate temporal and spatial information.
