For the Case B reference study, contact stress analysis based on ISO 6336–2:2006 produced an analytical value of 1302.34 MPa, compared with 1274.1 MPa from FEA, showing a deviation of approximately 2.2%. Parametric analysis demonstrated that increasing the face width from 20 to 30 mm reduced bending stress from 275.95 MPa to 183.96 MPa and improved the factor of safety from 5.89 to 9.30. A functional prototype integrating turning, drilling, and milling operations was successfully developed. The single-motor transmission architecture is expected to reduce energy consumption relative to separate single-purpose machines, and results in a compact machine design; this expectation is design-based rather than measured, as no efficiency measurements were recorded on the fabricated prototype. The proposed methodology confirms that analytical design combined with FEA provides a reliable framework for developing high-performance multifunctional CNC systems suitable for modern precision manufacturing.

title: Geological substrate and multi-factor controls on RUSLE-estimated water erosion in the Kuye River Basin over 25 years
summary: Quantifying the spatiotemporal dynamics of soil erosion and clarifying its associated driving factors are essential prerequisites for developing targeted soil and water conservation strategies. This study focused on the Kuye River Basin, a
content: Quantifying the spatiotemporal dynamics of soil erosion and clarifying its associated driving factors are essential prerequisites for developing targeted soil and water conservation strategies. This study focused on the Kuye River Basin, a primary coarse sediment source in the middle Yellow River. The RUSLE model was used to estimate the soil erosion modulus from 2000 to 2024, and the spatiotemporal evolution and geological differentiation of erosion were analyzed. An interpretable XGBoost-SHAP machine learning framework was constructed, incorporating climatic, topographic, vegetation, anthropogenic, and geological substrate factors, to quantitatively disentangle the contributions of each factor to the RUSLE-estimated erosion spatial pattern. Seven groups of controlled experiments were designed to examine the structural overlap between RUSLE internal factors and model independent variables. The results show that: (1) The overall soil erosion intensity exhibited an improving trend, but the spatial pattern remained stable with a pronounced lithological gradient. Aeolian loess, argillaceous rock, and clastic rock interbedded with argillaceous rock units were identified as persistent high erosion risk zones. (2) Geological substrate was the background factor most closely related to the spatial differentiation of erosion. The spatial distribution of single-factor sensitivity showed that high-sensitivity areas of the K factor coincided with argillaceous rock and aeolian sand, high-sensitivity areas of the LS factor were consistent with steep-slope zones in the loess hilly-gully region, and high-sensitivity areas of the C factor overlapped with low-vegetation-cover areas in the middle and lower reaches. The spatial superposition of these three factors is closely associated with the persistently high erosion risk in the high-risk units. The basin-wide erosion rebound in 2020 under extreme rainfall highlights the sensitivity of soft substrates to extreme climate. (3) Within the RUSLE framework, NDVI and slope, corresponding to the C and LS factors, contributed most to the spatial pattern of erosion modulus. However, controlled experiments indicated that this result partly arises from the mathematical structural relationship of the RUSLE equation, and the model performance primarily reflects its capacity to reconstruct RUSLE outputs under random holdout validation rather than cross-regional predictive transferability. External environmental variables (PET, Distance to roads, Distance to water, Aspect, Soil thickness, and Lithology) showed limited independent explanatory power for RUSLE outputs (M5 R 2 = – 0.011). Therefore, the SHAP results should be interpreted as the “covariate importance of the RUSLE-estimated erosion pattern” rather than the “causal mechanisms of actual erosion processes.” It is recommended that geological unit differentiation be incorporated as a core consideration in future soil and water conservation planning, and that a precision g

title: Influence of nickel and molybdenum disulfide additives on the microstructure and tribological performance of FeCrMoCB amorphous coatings fabricated by laser cladding
summary: The longevity and performance of industrial components are frequently compromised by surface wear, especially in high‐stress applications. This study explores the enhancement of Fe‐based coatings through the incorporation of nickel (Ni) and
content: The longevity and performance of industrial components are frequently compromised by surface wear, especially in high‐stress applications. This study explores the enhancement of Fe‐based coatings through the incorporation of nickel (Ni) and molybdenum disulfide (MoS 2 ) as alloying elements in nanoparticles size, utilizing laser cladding techniques. Nickel and molybdenum disulfide each independently improve coating performance by refining microstructures, enhancing toughness, and providing solid lubrication, respectively. The modified coatings were thoroughly assessed in terms of their microstructure, hardness, as well as resistance to wear. Coatings samples with 4 wt.% nickel (S2) and 4 wt.% molybdenum disulfide (S3) demonstrated significant improvements, including a 62.5 % reduction in wear volume loss and a 43.2 % decrease in the coefficient of friction compared to unmodified coatings. These findings highlight the potential of nickel and molybdenum disulfide additives in developing high‐performance coatings for demanding industrial environments.

title: Water Depollution Studies for the Removal of Contaminants Like Pesticides and Fluoride: Application to Real Water Samples
summary: ABSTRACT The ubiquitous use of pesticides in agricultural ecosystems is crucial for pest management, but it can lead to significant environmental contamination, particularly of freshwater resources. We report the successful adsorption effic
content: ABSTRACT The ubiquitous use of pesticides in agricultural ecosystems is crucial for pest management, but it can lead to significant environmental contamination, particularly of freshwater resources. We report the successful adsorption efficiency of a glass fiber–ferrite–PANI composite synthesized via an in situ polymerization method using lime juice as a dopant and reaction medium. UV–visible adsorption studies demonstrated excellent adsorption capacity for the target pollutants, with removal efficiencies ranging from 70% to 80%. Simultaneously, the NiFe constituent exhibited rapid and selective fluoride sequestration from aqueous media. Real water sample analyses further demonstrated the robust practical utility of the materials in mitigating target pollutants under complex environmental matrix conditions. Reusability assessments revealed exceptional chemical stability and removal efficiency across multiple consecutive adsorption–desorption cycles.

title: Cooperative multi-agent deep reinforcement learning for robust frequency regulation in renewable-integrated power systems
summary: This paper proposes a multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient with prioritized experience replay and cooperative gradient sharing (MADDPG-PER-Coop) framework for automatic generation control (AGC) in renewable-integrated interconnect
content: This paper proposes a multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient with prioritized experience replay and cooperative gradient sharing (MADDPG-PER-Coop) framework for automatic generation control (AGC) in renewable-integrated interconnected power systems. The proposed approach integrates prioritized experience replay, adaptive exploration noise, cooperative gradient sharing, State-of-Energy observation augmentation, and a composite multi-objective reward function to improve frequency regulation and tie-line power control under varying operating conditions. The framework is investigated using a three-area thermal–hydro–wind–solar photovoltaic interconnected power system and further examined in an extended five-area configuration to assess its performance under increased system dimensionality. Under the nominal benchmark condition, the proposed controller achieves a settling time of 8.0 s, an overshoot of 2.1%, an integral squared error (ISE) of (8.6\times10^{-3}), and an integral of time-weighted absolute error (ITAE) of 0.21. Compared with the conventional proportional–integral–derivative (PID) controller, these results correspond to reductions of 68.4%, 85.2%, 80.9%, and 76.4% in settling time, overshoot, ISE, and ITAE, respectively. In a separate stochastic evaluation involving 30 independent simulation runs, the proposed method achieves a mean ITAE of 0.248 with a standard deviation of 0.015 and a mean settling time of 5.94 s. The ablation analysis examines the contribution of the individual framework components to the observed control performance. In addition, real-time implementation using a dSPACE DS1104 platform yields a mean execution latency of 1.86 ms and a maximum latency of 2.47 ms, with peak frequency deviations of approximately 0.010–0.012 Hz across the evaluated areas. The results indicate that the proposed framework provides effective frequency regulation under the investigated simulation conditions and demonstrates real-time execution feasibility on the tested platform. The findings are limited to the evaluated system configurations and operating scenarios, and further assessment is required to establish its applicability to larger and more diverse power systems.

title: Freeze-Out Clock in TMC-1: Accretion Time Against Chemical Age and Free-Fall Time
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: This paper evaluates whether the time a CO molecule survives in the gas before striking a grain is short or long compared with the free-fall time and with commonly quoted chemical ages for this core in TMC-1 cyanopolyyne peak, using publish
content: This paper evaluates whether the time a CO molecule survives in the gas before striking a grain is short or long compared with the free-fall time and with commonly quoted chemical ages for this core in TMC-1 cyanopolyyne peak, using published physical conditions as fixed inputs rather than fitted parameters. The adopted molecular hydrogen density is 2e+04 per cubic centimetre at 10 K. From those inputs the freeze-out time for carbon monoxide is 2.9e+05 yr, compared with a free-fall time of 2.17e+08 yr, giving a ratio of 0.0013. The critical density of the reference transition is 2.4e+03 per cubic centimetre, so the core density exceeds it by a factor of 8.33. The depletion factor implied by the canonical and observed abundances is 2.83, leaving a gas fraction of 0.353. Thermal desorption balances accretion only near 20 K, well above the adopted temperature, while the cosmic-ray desorption time is 3e+05 yr and the representative gas-phase reaction time is 1 yr. Together these numbers place the chemistry of TMC-1 cyanopolyyne peak in a definite regime: accretion and ion-molecule processing are fast enough to shape the observed composition, thermal return is negligible, and any sustained gas-phase presence of strongly bound species must be maintained by non-thermal return or by incomplete exposure time. All values are computed from the stated inputs with the deposited code.

title: Covariation Impacts of the Western Pacific and Indian Subtropical Highs on Biomass Burning in the Greater Mekong Subregion
summary: Abstract This study investigated that the interannual covariation of Western Pacific Subtropical High (WPSH) and Indian Subtropical High (ISH) influences the biomass burning (BB) in the Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS) during the pre‐monsoon
content: Abstract This study investigated that the interannual covariation of Western Pacific Subtropical High (WPSH) and Indian Subtropical High (ISH) influences the biomass burning (BB) in the Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS) during the pre‐monsoon season (March–April). The analysis revealed that when the WPSH and ISH strengthen together, they tend to merge into an interconnected anticyclone that extends from the Indian Subcontinent to the South China Sea. This merged anticyclone enhances large‐scale subsidence, suppresses moisture transport from the Bay of Bengal and South China Sea, reduces precipitation and higher temperature across the GMS. Sensitivity experiments indicate that precipitation reduction is the primary driver of increased fire risk across most of the region, while strengthened winds facilitate the spread of BB in northern Laos. These drier and warmer conditions increase the Fire Weather Index (FWI) across 76.4% of the region, and lead to an increase in the BB frequency over 74.4% of the GMS. Croplands exhibit a significant increase in BB activity during the concurrent intensification of the WPSH and ISH, with BB frequency rising by ∼22% compared with the opposite phase. These results provide insights into the physical mechanisms of BB variability on the interannual time scale and potential pathways for preventing destructive BB.

title: Control of Metal–Support Interactions for Photocatalyst in Methane Conversion: Synthesis, Characterization, and Regulation
summary: necessitates on-site conversion. Conventional steam reforming demands extreme temperatures and pressures, incurring high energy penalties. Photocatalysis uses photon energy to drive methane conversion under milder conditions and can improve
content: necessitates on-site conversion. Conventional steam reforming demands extreme temperatures and pressures, incurring high energy penalties. Photocatalysis uses photon energy to drive methane conversion under milder conditions and can improve product selectivity through catalyst design. Wide-bandgap, thermally robust metal oxides have emerged as promising photocatalysts, but their intrinsic activity is modest and must be boosted by surface metal decoration. Such decoration initiates metal-support interactions (MSI) that govern charge transfer and surface kinetics, ultimately dictating photocatalytic methane conversion efficiency. This review first outlines synthetic strategies for creating MSI structures and summarizes state-of-the-art characterization tools for probing MSI phenomena and their catalytic consequences. We then classify MSI effects into four types: charge transfer, interfacial perimeter, morphology, and chemical composition and dissect their individual roles in photocatalytic methane conversion. This review concludes with design principles and future perspectives for engineering MSI architectures toward efficient photocatalytic methane valorization.

title: Recognizing the Versatility of Heterogeneous Catalysts Can Provide New Opportunities
summary: Abstract Heterogeneous catalysts are most often designed to facilitate a specific reaction. We propose that evaluating one catalyst across several reactions is advantageous to make more efficient use of resources and increasing the data gen
content: Abstract Heterogeneous catalysts are most often designed to facilitate a specific reaction. We propose that evaluating one catalyst across several reactions is advantageous to make more efficient use of resources and increasing the data generated for machine learning. Screening a single material for potential catalytic activity across multiple reactions and operating conditions samples a substantially wider region of the reaction condition parameter space than a single optimization. This can produce a multitude of performance metrics for an identically prepared and characterized material. Current literature reporting practices are biased toward reporting only optimal experimental outcomes. In practice, results obtained from low-conversion and low-selectivity catalysts would likely constrain a regression model to a similar degree as would data obtained from a high-performing catalyst, but these are seldom published. Systematically recording the full distribution of outcomes produces data sets that are better suited at modeling structure–property relationships, and support multitask learning, in which data from several reactions inform a shared representation of the catalyst. We showcase this by taking Pd/ZnO and Cu/ZnO that are effective for CO2 hydrogenation and applying them to other diverse reactions such as preferential oxidation of CO and photocatalytic ibuprofen decomposition in water. We find that Cu/ZnO and CuO/ZnO were more effective than Pd/ZnO in facilitating both the CO preferential oxidation reaction and ibuprofen decomposition. The versatility of the Cu-based catalyst demonstrates the potential for future studies that involve a broader approach whereby heterogeneous catalysts can be specifically repurposed for multiple processes.

title: From brittle to ductile: synergistic effects of EPS waste and polypropylene fibers in reduced-density concrete with strength–density optimization
summary: The incorporation of expanded polystyrene (EPS) waste into concrete reduces density but typically compromises compressive strength due to increased porosity and weak interfacial transition zones. This study investigates a hybrid modificatio
content: The incorporation of expanded polystyrene (EPS) waste into concrete reduces density but typically compromises compressive strength due to increased porosity and weak interfacial transition zones. This study investigates a hybrid modification strategy combining EPS (5–20% fine aggregate replacement) and polypropylene (PP) fibers (0.9% by cement weight) to mitigate strength degradation while enhancing tensile performance. Thirty cylindrical specimens (150 × 300 mm) were tested at 28 days for compressive and split tensile strength. Results indicate that compressive strength decreased moderately from 27 MPa (control) to 24.13–25.32 MPa. Corrected split tensile strength values ranged from 0.69 to 0.92 MPa, which are physically consistent with concrete of this compressive strength range and do not indicate enhancement over control (0.72 MPa). Density reduction reached 5.95% at 20% EPS, which classifies the material as reduced-density normal-weight concrete rather than lightweight concrete, since all densities (2213–2353 kg/m³) exceed the ACI 213R lightweight threshold of 1850 kg/m³. One-way ANOVA confirmed significant differences among mix types ( p < 0.05); however, because the control contained no fiber while all EPS mixes contained fiber, the individual effects of EPS and PP fiber cannot be statistically separated in this design. A multi-objective strength–density optimization index (SPI) was developed to quantify performance efficiency, identifying 5% EPS as the first-peak optimum in the strength–density trade-off. The findings demonstrate that fiber reinforcement may contribute to crack control through bridging mechanisms, though the confounding of EPS and fiber in the mix design prevents isolation of this effect. The proposed hybrid approach provides a sustainable pathway for plastic waste valorization in non-structural and semi-structural concrete applications.

title: Adhesive Interaction of Polymeric Ligands With the γ‐ Al 2 O 3 Surface as a Basis for Searching for Stable Catalysts for Fischer–Tropsch Synthesis: Quantum Chemistry and Molecular Dynamics
summary: ABSTRACT The adhesive interaction of polymeric ligands (poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET), poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA), poly(propylene carbonate) (PPC), polystyrene (PS), and polypropylene (PP)) with the oxidized aluminum surface (γ‐A
content: ABSTRACT The adhesive interaction of polymeric ligands (poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET), poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA), poly(propylene carbonate) (PPC), polystyrene (PS), and polypropylene (PP)) with the oxidized aluminum surface (γ‐Al 2 O 3 )—which models the real support of Fischer–Tropsch synthesis catalysts—was systematically investigated using quantum chemistry (PBE‐GD3/MOLOPT with PIEDA analysis) and molecular dynamics (PCFF and IFF force fields). On the γ‐Al 2 O 3 surface, adhesion occurs via donor–acceptor bonds formed between carbonyl and ether oxygen atoms and aluminum atoms, with the dominant contributions to the adhesion energy coming from electrostatic and donor–acceptor components. The calculated work of adhesion on the γ‐Al 2 O 3 surface decreases in the order PET > PPC > PMMA > PS > PP. The obtained ranking of adhesion strength is in good agreement with the experimental acid–base surface characteristics and provides a quantitative basis for the rational selection of polymeric ligands that ensure maximum stability of hybrid Fischer–Tropsch synthesis catalysts on γ‐Al 2 O 3 supports.

title: Closing the Loop From Manufacturing Defects to Field Failures: Root Causes, Detection, and Quality Control Strategies for Preventing Thermal Runaway in Lithium‐Ion Batteries
summary: ABSTRACT Lithium‐ion batteries power consumer electronics, electric vehicles, and stationary energy‐storage systems, yet rare catastrophic failures associated with thermal runaway remain a significant safety concern. Many such failures orig
content: ABSTRACT Lithium‐ion batteries power consumer electronics, electric vehicles, and stationary energy‐storage systems, yet rare catastrophic failures associated with thermal runaway remain a significant safety concern. Many such failures originate from latent manufacturing defects, including metallic contaminants, coating non‐uniformities, electrode burrs, misalignment, separator damage, defective tab welds, and moisture contamination. These defects may escape conventional end‐of‐line inspection and remain dormant until electrochemical, thermal, or mechanical stresses promote internal short circuits, localized heating, or other failure mechanisms. Existing reviews generally address either defect formation, internal short‐circuit mechanisms, or production inspection methods, but rarely connect these topics across the complete failure lifecycle. This review establishes a closed‐loop framework linking defect generation during manufacturing to detection, field failure, root‐cause analysis, and corrective action. Manufacturing defects are classified according to their process origin and evaluated in terms of potential safety consequences. In‐line inspection, electrical screening, imaging, non‐destructive evaluation, and data‐driven quality‐control approaches are critically examined with emphasis on their detection capabilities and limitations. A systematic methodology for field‐failure analysis is also presented, incorporating initial triage, non‐destructive examination, controlled disassembly, physicochemical characterization, production traceability, and root‐cause assessment. Representative incidents involving consumer electronics, aviation, electric vehicles, and stationary energy‐storage systems are used to illustrate how manufacturing defects, design margins, inspection limitations, and system‐level factors can interact in service. Finally, gaps between conventional safety qualification and rare latent‐defect detection are discussed, together with priorities for predictive monitoring, integrated production and field data, and closed‐loop quality systems capable of improving battery safety as manufacturing scale and cell technologies continue to evolve.

title: A multiscale framework for the design and analysis of energy systems in Bolivia
summary: Abstract Large-scale technology transitions entail the simultaneous adoption of technologies and dependent resources, as well as a shift in policy and human capital. Systems often consist of multiple interdependent processes, allowing decis
content: Abstract Large-scale technology transitions entail the simultaneous adoption of technologies and dependent resources, as well as a shift in policy and human capital. Systems often consist of multiple interdependent processes, allowing decisions to propagate through subsystems. Moreover, systems operate under uncertainty and are influenced by phenomena occurring at different temporal and spatial scales. To​ this end,​ a ​multiscale​ and​ multi-product​ analytical framework is required for informed decision-making. Such a framework is presented to analyze transition scenarios for Bolivia. The presented work​ explores the impact of replacing natural gas technologies on energy security and cost-effectiveness of Bolivia. Using a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming optimization model, we evaluate various energy scenarios wherein the system is given the option to adopt alternative technologies, viz. biomass, hydropower, oil, and variable renewable energy (VRE) sources such as solar and wind. Our analysis identifies hydropower and biomass as the most viable alternatives. Notably, VREs are burdened by the need for a high capital investment resulting from limited resource and technology availability. The study provides valuable insight into Bolivia’s energy challenges, offering a user-adaptable model for future energy planning and policy decisions aimed at building more sustainable and resilient energy systems. The proposed methodology is adaptable to other countries, offering a systematic tool to guide sustainable energy transitions.

title: A self‐amplifying antimicrobial nanoagent: ALASe combines dark toxicity with in situ porphyrin biosynthesis for enhanced antimicrobial photodynamic therapy
summary: Abstract The rise of multidrug‐resistant bacteria demands innovative antimicrobial strategies that combine multiple mechanisms of action. Selenium nanoparticles functionalized with 5‐aminolevulinic acid (ALASe) offer a dual‐action platform,
content: Abstract The rise of multidrug‐resistant bacteria demands innovative antimicrobial strategies that combine multiple mechanisms of action. Selenium nanoparticles functionalized with 5‐aminolevulinic acid (ALASe) offer a dual‐action platform, coupling the intrinsic bactericidal activity of selenium with photodynamic toxicity derived from metabolically generated porphyrins. ALASe nanoparticles were synthesized via a one‐pot photoreduction method and characterized by TEM, DLS, XRD, FTIR, 1 H NMR, HRMS, ICP‐OES, and fluorescence spectroscopy. The resulting nanoparticles were spherical, 180–220 nm in size, with moderate colloidal stability (zeta potential ≈ −26 mV) and fluorescence emission at 514 nm. Antibacterial activity was evaluated against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus under dark and blue‐light (460 nm) conditions. ALASe exhibited dose‐dependent dark toxicity against both strains, confirming an intrinsic selenium‐mediated antibacterial effect. Upon blue‐light irradiation, bacterial inactivation was significantly enhanced, consistent with metabolic conversion of ALA into photoactive porphyrins. Intracellular porphyrin accumulation was confirmed by fluorescence spectroscopy, and photodynamic efficacy correlated directly with porphyrin levels. Singlet oxygen generation was further quantified by phosphorescence decay analysis of porphyrins extracted from ALASe‐incubated bacteria, confirming the photosensitizing role of the accumulated porphyrins. Together, these results demonstrate that ALASe combines two complementary antibacterial mechanisms: selenium‐dependent dark toxicity and a light‐activatable photodynamic response driven by bacterial conversion of ALA to porphyrin. This dual‐mechanism positions ALASe as a promising multifunctional nanoplatform for combating antibiotic‐resistant infections, particularly in superficial or topical applications where light delivery is feasible.

title: Pre-synthesis theoretical study of acetophenone and indole adsorption on fullerene nanocage derivatives for their removal and separation from wastewater
summary: This study evaluates pristine C60 and its B- and Si-substituted derivatives (BC59 and SiC59), as theoretically proposed platforms for adsorbing acetophenone (ACF) and indole (IDO) in wastewater and for studying their adsorption-induced elec
content: This study evaluates pristine C60 and its B- and Si-substituted derivatives (BC59 and SiC59), as theoretically proposed platforms for adsorbing acetophenone (ACF) and indole (IDO) in wastewater and for studying their adsorption-induced electronic and optical responses. We performed calculations using the B97D and ωB97X-D functionals. We examined structural stability through cohesive-energy and vibrational analyses, and characterized adsorption using optimized geometries, BSSE-corrected adsorption energies, estimated recovery times, frontier-orbital descriptors, dipole moments, a dimensionless gap-based electronic-response descriptor proxy, TD-DFT spectra, NBO, QTAIM, ELF, and LOL analyses. Pristine C 60 interacted weakly with both analytes, yielding corrected adsorption energies of approximately −6.6 to −7.1 kcal.mol −1 and predominantly closed-shell, noncovalent contacts. Substitution with B or Si considerably strengthened the predicted adsorption by creating localized electron-accepting sites. At the ωB97X-D level, adsorption energies reached −19.80 and −26.22 kcal.mol −1 for BC59@IDO and SiC 59 @IDO and −22.23 and −34.64 kcal.mol −1 for BC 59 @ACF and SiC59@ACF, respectively. NBO and QTAIM results together indicated localized, strongly polarized N···B/Si and O···B/Si contacts, with partial shared-electron contributions according to the QTAIM energy–density criteria. Adsorption also produced pronounced frontier-orbital changes, with dimensionless gap-based response values (Rg) reaching + 4.139 for BC59@IDO at the ωB97X-D level and + 6.788 for SiC59@ACF at the B97D level. BC59@ACF was additionally predicted to have a visible-region absorption maximum at 605.44 nm. Overall, SiC59 gave the strongest predicted adsorption and the largest B97D gap-based response for ACF, whereas BC59 offered a potentially more balanced adsorption-recovery response. These results provide a pre-synthesis basis for future experimental evaluation of the proposed fullerene-based platforms.

title: From Thermal Thresholds to Temporal Response: A Dual‐Dimension Framework for Lithium‐Ion Battery Safety
summary: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) face a persistent safety challenge from thermal runaway (TR), a catastrophic failure triggered by exothermic chain reactions under abuse conditions. Despite extensive progress in material-level thermal stabiliza
content: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) face a persistent safety challenge from thermal runaway (TR), a catastrophic failure triggered by exothermic chain reactions under abuse conditions. Despite extensive progress in material-level thermal stabilization, most strategies remain confined to raising temperature thresholds, overlooking the temporal dimension of TR progression. This review introduces a temperature-time dual-dimensional framework that unifies TR mechanisms, characterization techniques, and mitigation strategies. We first elucidate the TR process and put forward key parameters. Meanwhile, a thermal-electrochemical-chemical (TEC) coupling model is constructed that reveals three intervention windows: decoupling (temperature-prioritized), interruption (time-prioritized), and containment (system-level). We then survey characterization methods across material and cell levels, followed by a critical assessment of temperature- and time-domain strategies, ranging from thermally stable materials to smart electrolytes, PTC collectors, and self-responsive separators. We construct a design space that map strategies by their ΔT and Δt effectiveness, highlighting the trade-off between temperature stability and time responsiveness. Finally, we outline three strategic frontiers, that is, multifunctional materials, machine learning-enabled prediction, and self-reporting/self-healing systems, to guide future development. This framework provides a roadmap for intrinsically safe LIBs, bridging fundamental materials design and practical battery engineering.

title: Topological Superlattice Stabilized Layered Oxide Cathodes With Sustainable Anionic Redox
summary: ABSTRACT Harnessing the oxygen anionic redox (OAR) at high voltage is envisaged as a fascinating approach to promote the energy density of rechargeable batteries. However, the layered transition metal (TM) oxide cathode materials with OAR a
content: ABSTRACT Harnessing the oxygen anionic redox (OAR) at high voltage is envisaged as a fascinating approach to promote the energy density of rechargeable batteries. However, the layered transition metal (TM) oxide cathode materials with OAR activity suffer severely from detrimental phase transformations and local structural disorders, leading to electrochemical performance degradation. Herein, we propose a topological superlattice regulation strategy to construct a cathode material with the Li/Mg/Ni‐triple‐center honeycomb superlattice for sodium‐ion batteries. The combined theoretical and in/ex situ investigations demonstrate that the Li/Mg‐centered superlattice topology activates the OAR reaction to boost specific capacity, while the Ni‐centered honeycomb motif prevents the lattice oxygen release by increasing the TM−O covalency. Furthermore, the multi‐topology superlattice configuration suppresses the P−O phase transition and Li/TM interlayer/intralayer migration to reinforce the honeycomb superstructure stability, improving the oxygen redox reversibility. Consequently, the topological superlattice‐stabilized cathode delivers a high capacity of 242 mAh g −1 and exhibits outstanding cycling stability (91.8% capacity retention after 100 cycles). This work provides new insights into the superstructure regulation of state‐of‐the‐art cathode materials for sustainable batteries.

title: Non‐Precious Metal High‐Entropy Oxide Sub‐1 nm Nanowires for Li‐O 2 Batteries
summary: ABSTRACT Highly active and structurally robust cathode catalysts are critically required to boost the electrochemical performance of lithium‐oxygen batteries (LOBs). Herein, a generally synthetic method of non‐precious metal high‐entropy ox
content: ABSTRACT Highly active and structurally robust cathode catalysts are critically required to boost the electrochemical performance of lithium‐oxygen batteries (LOBs). Herein, a generally synthetic method of non‐precious metal high‐entropy oxide‐polyoxometalate sub‐1 nm nanowires (NPMHEO‐POM SNWs) has been successfully developed induced by POM clusters under mild solvothermal conditions. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations reveal that the dominantly driving forces for the assembly of POMs and multi‐metal oxides are the Coulomb and van der Waals forces, enabling precise theoretical guidance for targeted material synthesis. Benefiting from the 1D ultrafine structure with fully exposed active sites, the precise adjustment of components optimizing the adsorption capability of intermediate (LiO 2 *) and discharge product (Li 2 O 2 ), and the strong interactions of multi‐metal oxides and POMs contributing to the stability, the BiVZrNiCeO x ‐phosphomolybdic acid SNWs‐based LOB achieves a highly specific capacity of 9944 mAh g −1 and stable cycling durability for 312 cycles at 500 mA g −1 , highlighting their great promise as high‐efficiency electrocatalysts for advanced LOBs.

title: Synthesis of MWCNTs by Chemical Vapor Deposition from Kerosene
source: Science Forum (Journal of Pure and Applied Sciences)
summary: A carbon nanotubes CNTs with less then 7 sheets of Graphene ( few walled according to classification of carbon tubes with Nano scales) were prepared by chemical vapor deposition from kerosene as sources of carbon. The prepared carbon nano m
content: A carbon nanotubes CNTs with less then 7 sheets of Graphene ( few walled according to classification of carbon tubes with Nano scales) were prepared by chemical vapor deposition from kerosene as sources of carbon. The prepared carbon nano materials was SP2 hybridization consisting of tubes with nano meter for radius and micro meters in lengths and homogeneous in distributions . The identifications were represent by Raman spectroscopy, FT-IR, and XPS for detect nature of of function groups while crystalline of tubular structures was done by X-ray diffraction XRD while stability of structure was achieved with thermogravimetric analysis TGA. The outer morphology and detection outer and inner diameters were taken by electron microscopy with scanning techniques (SEM). The average values was 13 nm and 6 nm for outer and inner diameters respectively and that refers to 4-7 graphene sheets and lengths were more then 1 µm .

title: Vagal afferent activation induces a dissociated NREM sleep-like state with wake-related locus coeruleus activity
summary: Abstract Parasympathetic nervous system activity, vital for restorative sleep, is influenced by vagal sensory afferents, but how these shape brain-body correlates of sleep remains open. Here we combined vagal sensory neuron (VSN) stimulatio
content: Abstract Parasympathetic nervous system activity, vital for restorative sleep, is influenced by vagal sensory afferents, but how these shape brain-body correlates of sleep remains open. Here we combined vagal sensory neuron (VSN) stimulation in the mouse with EEG/EMG, heart rate, brain-body temperature, noradrenergic locus coeruleus (LC) neuron population activity measures and in vitro synaptic physiology to investigate the effects of VSN activation on sleep-wake states. We show that chemogenetic VSN stimulation during the resting phase induced a non-rapid-eye-movement sleep (NREMS)-like state with enriched, but homeostatically regulated, low-frequency (0.75–4 Hz) EEG activity, yet suppressed REMS. Simultaneously, brain-body temperatures dropped while LC activity increased. The gradual recovery towards normal NREMS-REMS-cycles was accelerated by external warming, identifying cooling as key contributing factor. We conclude that VSN activation can promote brain-body correlates as a continuum of normal NREMS while engaging wake-promoting forebrain neuromodulation, revealing a coexistence of classically incompatible sleep- and wake-associated signatures.

title: Fresh tephra deposits from the Tajogaite Volcano boost thermophile proliferation and soil organic matter recovery
summary: Tephra fallout deposition during volcanic eruptions overlays existing soils, profoundly altering their physical, chemical, and biological properties. This study investigates the impact of the newly deposited tephra blanket from the 2021 Taj
content: Tephra fallout deposition during volcanic eruptions overlays existing soils, profoundly altering their physical, chemical, and biological properties. This study investigates the impact of the newly deposited tephra blanket from the 2021 Tajogaite eruption (La Palma Island) on the molecular composition of soil organic matter and microbial diversity across different soil horizons. To our knowledge, this is the first study combining molecular pyrolysis, stable isotope analysis, and microbial sequencing to characterize the early biogeochemical transformation of soils affected by the Tajogaite eruption. A combination of 16S rRNA gene sequencing, pyrolysis-gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (Py-GC/MS), and elemental and isotope ratio mass spectrometry (EA/IRMS) was employed. Our results reveal marked differences in organic matter composition and microbial community structure across the tephra-covered soil profile, with patterns consistent with ongoing microbial transformation of organic carbon and nitrogen compounds. The soil horizon directly beneath the tephra layer (horizon O) displayed a higher abundance of labile organic compounds and a reduced presence of recalcitrant compounds compared to the deeper horizons (A and Bw). This pattern is strongly associated with the predominance of thermophilic bacteria, which contribute actively to the breakdown of complex organic materials such as lignin and hydrocarbons, and drive key biogeochemical processes including nitrogen and carbon cycling. The continuous geothermal influence of nearby fumaroles further supports the persistence and ecological success of thermophilic communities in these volcanic soils. These findings underscore the critical role of volcanic activity not only in reshaping soil structure but also in enhancing soil fertility and resilience through microbial-mediated processes. Understanding these dynamics is essential for soil management and ecosystem recovery strategies in volcanic regions, providing new insights into the long-term effects of tephra deposition on soil health and the carbon cycle.

title: Assessing Early-Stage Net CO 2 Fluxes From Soils and Maize Plants During a Short-Term Enhanced Weathering Mesocosm Trial
summary: It is becoming increasingly accepted that annual gigatonne-scale carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) removal, in conjunction with rapid decarbonization, is necessary to meet international climate goals and limit global warming below 2 °C. This will requ
content: It is becoming increasingly accepted that annual gigatonne-scale carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) removal, in conjunction with rapid decarbonization, is necessary to meet international climate goals and limit global warming below 2 °C. This will require the development and rapid scaling of new forms of carbon management. When developing new carbon dioxide removal (CDR) techniques, complete accounting of how the process affects greenhouse gas fluxes is essential. Enhanced weathering (EW), the spreading of weatherable, cation-rich crushed rocks to soils, has the potential to sequester significant amounts of CO 2 while improving soil health. Yet, the effect that increases in soil pH from EW has on soil organic carbon (SOC) decomposition remains debated. A potential concern is that increasing soil pH can lead to enhanced SOC remineralization, although more data is needed. Additionally, many studies do not measure CO 2 fluxes continuously, capture net top-of-column CO 2 fluxes, or monitor established key levers on CO 2 emission from soils. To add to this debate, we present soil carbon pool data from a ~3 month time series encompassing sequential net CO 2 flux experiments from an EW greenhouse study in large mesocosms. We focused on mildly acidic soils where, on short time scales, cations from weathering quantitively moved into the exchangeable fraction. Therefore, gas flux changes in this system should be largely linked to changes in organic carbon (SOC stores and plant processes). We find no significant correlation between CO 2 fluxes and soil pH and no significant correlation between CO 2 fluxes and rock application. Although this does not rule out a link between soil pH and SOC remineralization rates, the effect is small relative to other factors, like temperature and soil moisture. Although minor increases in total inorganic carbon were observed in basalt-amended soils, these increases did not support a direct link between soil pH and increased CO 2 emissions.

title: Unravelling groundwater's role in soil-plant-atmosphere continuum: integrated ecohydrological modelling approach using STEMMUS-SCOPE and MODFLOW 6
summary: Soil-plant-atmosphere continuum (SPAC) models are commonly used to investigate various components' role(s) in ecosystem functioning. Yet, in most SPAC models, groundwater is ignored or at best represented in an over-simplified manner, leadi
content: Soil-plant-atmosphere continuum (SPAC) models are commonly used to investigate various components' role(s) in ecosystem functioning. Yet, in most SPAC models, groundwater is ignored or at best represented in an over-simplified manner, leading to misunderstanding of its critical role in simulating soil-vegetation dynamics. This study investigates groundwater's role in SPAC processes, in particular, the impacts of groundwater component (mass and energy) on: (1) regulating the soil profile, in terms of moisture and temperature; (2) the dynamics of the unsaturated/saturated zones and their further impact on water fluxes; and (3) the carbon fluxes and vegetation physiological processes (i.e. root water uptake and photosynthesis reflected by fluorescence). To address this, an integrated ecohydrological modelling (IEM) framework is developed by coupling the STEMMUS-SCOPE SPAC model with the MODFLOW 6 integrated hydrological model. The standalone STEMMUS-SCOPE (ST-SC) and the coupled STEMMUS-SCOPE-MODFLOW 6 (ST-SC-MF6) models were applied over an 8-year period (1 April 2016–31 March 2024) to three sites in the Netherlands (Loobos, Cabauw and Veenkampen). Various essential variables, including soil moisture ( θ ), soil temperature ( T s ), groundwater level (GWL), groundwater temperature (GT), evapotranspiration (ET), gross primary productivity (GPP), net ecosystem exchange (NEE), and sun-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) were simulated and then compared to corresponding in-situ observations. Performance of both ST-SC and ST-SC-MF6 was evaluated using the Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) and the root mean square error (RMSE) metrics. Results indicated that the groundwater contribution is spatially and temporally variable. The ST-SC-MF6 model showed better agreement with observations than the ST-SC, improving the KGE values for: (a) θ (+0.29), T s (+0.19), and ET (+0.35) at Loobos, (b) θ (+0.30), T s (+0.14), NEE (+0.18), and SIF (+0.15) at Cabauw, and (c) θ (+0.21) and ET (+0.15) at Veenkampen. Notably, benefits of ST-SC-MF6 simulation were particularly prominent during both wet and dry periods, i.e. improving the representation of: (a) the θ dynamics during wet conditions, when hydraulic connectivity between the phreatic surface and the unsaturated zone is strong; (b) the root water uptake and carbon assimilation during dry periods, when shallow groundwater mitigated vegetative water stress; and (c) the T s dynamics during both wet and dry periods, influenced by both GT and GWL, and further propagated to other T s -dependent processes/variables such as canopy temperature. Overall, the proposed ST-SC-MF6 IEM helped to: (1) incorporate groundwater as a key component of the water, energy and carbon cycles; and (2) define the important role groundwater dynamics plays in the SPAC for deepening the understanding of ecosystem functioning.

title: A hierarchical metabolic flux orchestrates cell cycle transitions in bacteria
summary: Mechanisms interlinking metabolic cues with cell cycle programs remain unknown. We show that an oscillating cytosolic redox critically governs cell cycle transitions in Caulobacter crescentus. By integrating evolutionary genetics with metab
content: Mechanisms interlinking metabolic cues with cell cycle programs remain unknown. We show that an oscillating cytosolic redox critically governs cell cycle transitions in Caulobacter crescentus. By integrating evolutionary genetics with metabolic flux tracing, we uncover temporally orchestrated shifts in core metabolic pathways that remodel cytosolic redox across the cell cycle. Early stages channel carbon flux toward unsaturated fatty-acid synthesis and a reverse-TCA to drive cytosolic oxidation-coupled G1-to-S transition. The later stages depend on an enhanced forward-TCA cycle that promote cytosolic reduction-driven proliferation. Strikingly, perturbing fatty-acid synthesis or reverse/forward-TCA cycle uncouples growth from proliferation. Intriguingly, a biphasic glucose uptake program dictates the cell cycle-stage-specific metabolism. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized metabolic-redox circuitry that coordinates cell cycle progression in bacteria. They further unveil several metabolic branchpoints as promising targets for chemical intervention to disrupt critical and conserved cell cycle events, with potential applicability to bacterial pathogens. How cells coordinate growth and division with their metabolic state is poorly understood. Here, Agrawal et al. describe changes in glucose uptake and central metabolism that alter cytosolic redox balance and drive cell cycle progression in the bacterial model Caulobacter crescentus.

title: Time-evolved hetero-alkali interphases enable long-life sulfide-based anode-free solid-state batteries
summary: Sulfide-based anode-free solid-state batteries (AFSSBs) offer high energy density and improved safety, but their practical implementation is hindered by parasitic reactions between freshly plated lithium (Li) and sulfide solid electrolytes.
content: Sulfide-based anode-free solid-state batteries (AFSSBs) offer high energy density and improved safety, but their practical implementation is hindered by parasitic reactions between freshly plated lithium (Li) and sulfide solid electrolytes. These reactions continuously consume the limited cathode-derived Li inventory, increase interfacial impedance, and promote nonuniform Li plating and stripping. Here, sodium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (NaFSI) is incorporated into Li 5.4 PS 4.4 Cl 1.6 (LPSC) to kinetically program interphase evolution. Heat treatment initially generates a NaF/LiF-rich interphase on the LPSC surface. This fluoride-rich region chemically stabilizes the interface and suppresses direct LPSC reduction. During the early cycles, the outermost region progressively evolves into a LiF/Li 3 N-rich layer, while the NaF-containing phase becomes buried beneath the Li-rich surface region, producing a time-evolved compositional gradient. Although NaF provides effective chemical passivation, its poor Li + conductivity can impede interfacial ion transport. The subsequent formation of Li 3 N-rich domains, which exhibit substantially higher Li + conductivity than NaF, provides more favorable transport pathways, homogenizes interfacial Li + flux, and promotes uniform Li plating and stripping. This time-evolved gradient interphase therefore combines early-stage chemical stabilization and Li conservation with improved long-term ion transport kinetics, suppressing impedance growth, localized inactive Li accumulation, and filamentary shorting. Consequently, the AFSSB using the NaFSI-modified LPSC interlayer retains 77.6% of its capacity after 500 cycles at 0.2 C, whereas the cell with bare LPSC retains only 32.1% after 100 cycles. These findings establish temporally programmed gradient interphases as a general strategy for conserving active Li and stabilizing sulfide-based AFSSBs.

title: Parametric Gravity Wave Forcings in the Stratocumulus-Topped Boundary Layer under a Prescribed Radiative-Convective Equilibrium
summary: Abstract This work studies the breakup propensity of the stratocumulus-topped boundary layer (STBL) interacting with gravity waves using large-eddy simulation with a uniform vertical grid of 5 m and horizontal spacing of 30 m. A radiative-c
content: Abstract This work studies the breakup propensity of the stratocumulus-topped boundary layer (STBL) interacting with gravity waves using large-eddy simulation with a uniform vertical grid of 5 m and horizontal spacing of 30 m. A radiative-convective equilibrium (RCE) state is constructed to enforce stationarity in the STBL, and the gravity waves are introduced via a vertical momentum forcing mimicking a packet of waves. A nondimensionalization involving the inversion height ( z i ) and mean horizontal base wind as length and velocity scales is proposed to provide a framework to analyze the forcing parameter space. The magnitude of the scaled forcing amplitude (𝒜) is critical in understanding various STBL breakup conditions. Classification of breakup was based on the reduction of the liquid water path for each forced STBL case. For 𝒜 < 1, breakup did not occur, while we observed modest cloud reductions for 1 < 𝒜 < 2. However, STBL-stationarity was gradually reestablished after the single-period forcing ceased. Fixing 𝒜 ∼ 2 showed that forcings with longer duration and an o ( z i ) vertical length scale promoted breakup. When the forcing has two intrinsic periods, the percentage of cleared cloud dramatically increased, though recovery towards RCE is still observed. 𝒜 ≥ 2.5 marks a critical threshold by which the STBL broke up entirely, but this is sensitive to the imposed longwave cooling time scale. We explore the connection between these bulk breakup results and the turbulent state by examining energy budgets and the anisotropy induced by the forcing.

title: Untargeted serum and cerebrospinal fluid metabolomics of apparently healthy rabies virus-positive dogs in Nigeria
summary: INTRODUCTION: Rabies remains a neglected zoonotic disease of global public health importance because of its near-universal fatality, limited reliable antemortem diagnostic options, and absence of effective treatment following the onset of c
content: INTRODUCTION: Rabies remains a neglected zoonotic disease of global public health importance because of its near-universal fatality, limited reliable antemortem diagnostic options, and absence of effective treatment following the onset of clinical signs. However, metabolic alterations in dogs that are rabies-positive but show no observable clinical signs remain poorly characterized. Therefore, this study aimed to identify differentially abundant metabolites in apparently clinically healthy, direct fluorescent antibody (DFA)-positive dogs compared with DFA-negative dogs. METHODOLOGY: Samples comprising brain tissue, serum, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were collected from 231 apparently clinically healthy dogs. Rabies virus antigen was detected in brain tissue using the direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test, and dogs were classified as rabies-positive or negative based on the results. Metabolites were extracted from serum and CSF using a validated sample preparation procedure for untargeted metabolomics. Metabolomic profiling was performed using comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography coupled with time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GC×GC-TOFMS) under optimized analytical conditions. RESULTS: Rabies virus antigen was detected in 20 of 231 brain tissue samples (8.7%). Corresponding serum and CSF samples were classified as rabies (DFA)-positive, while 20 negative samples were selected for comparison. After quality control, 868 serum and 300 CSF compounds were retained. Neither principal component analysis nor partial least squares discriminant analysis separated the groups in either matrix. Four serum features remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction: Analyte 634, glyceric acid and Analyte 706 were lower, and benzoic acid was higher, in DFA-positive dogs. Analyte 634 gave the highest discovery-set area under the curve (AUC = 0.9575). In CSF, one unannotated feature (Analyte 369) was lower in DFA-positive dogs after FDR correction. Serum Analyte 634 and CSF Analyte 369 share retention times and mass spectra and may be the same compound. The serum pathways with the lowest enrichment p-values were mapped mainly by glyceric acid alone, and no CSF pathway remained significant after FDR correction. Indolelactic acid was higher in DFA-positive dogs in both matrices at the nominal level only. CONCLUSION: Four serum features and one CSF feature differed between apparently healthy DFA-positive and DFA-negative dogs after FDR correction. These are discovery-stage candidate features that require structural confirmation, targeted quantification and validation in an independent cohort before any diagnostic claim can be made.

title: Raising mountains for a habitable Earth
summary: The formation of mountain belts (orogens) elevates rocks above sea level, making them available for chemical weathering and altering the composition of the atmosphere and oceans, which in turn control habitability. Peak-metamorphic pressure
content: The formation of mountain belts (orogens) elevates rocks above sea level, making them available for chemical weathering and altering the composition of the atmosphere and oceans, which in turn control habitability. Peak-metamorphic pressures recorded by crustal rocks buried in orogens increased between 2.7 to 2.2 and 0.8 to 0.7 billion years ago, indicating that rocks could be buried deeper and that orogens could grow substantially thicker after each of these periods. The two periods of orogenic growth were broadly synchronous with major increases in terrigenous element and nutrient fluxes and changes in biological sulfur metabolism and surface oxygenation. These changes could be explained by enhanced weathering of higher mountains. The findings support the hypothesis that there are first-order mechanistic links between secular geodynamic change and changes in Earth system state and habitability, which shaped the conditions for the evolution of complex life during the past 3 billion years.

title: Development of PEBA-PEMA blend membranes for the pervaporation separation of 1-butanol from aqueous solutions
summary: Using the Hansen’s solubility parameters (HSPs) approach, novel polyether block amide (PEBA)-polyethyl methacrylate (PEMA) polymer blend membranes were synthesized and applied for the pervaporation (PV) separation of 1-butanol. Blending wit
content: Using the Hansen’s solubility parameters (HSPs) approach, novel polyether block amide (PEBA)-polyethyl methacrylate (PEMA) polymer blend membranes were synthesized and applied for the pervaporation (PV) separation of 1-butanol. Blending with PEMA led to an increase in surface roughness and hydrophobicity. PV performance of the blend membranes for the recovery of 1-butanol from aqueous solution (20 g/L) at 40 °C showed an improvement in separation performance with the blending of PEMA; however, a higher blending ratio (≥ 8 wt%) significantly reduced PV performance due to phase separation. The membrane (PBPM-5) containing 5 wt% of PEMA achieved the best PV separation, yielding a flux of 0.19 kgm −2 h − 1 and a separation factor of 15.5, which is a 50% enhancement in flux and a twofold increase in the separation factor as compared to the pristine PEBA membrane. An increase in PV operation temperature and feed butanol content showed simultaneous enhancement in both the separation factor and flux for the PBPM-5 membrane. Separation of butanol from multicomponent mixture resulted in lower performance indicating the presence of strong coupling effect. This work shows the PV butanol separation capability of PEBA can be significantly enhanced through the judicious blending of small amount of PEMA polymer.

title: Phase Behavior of Thermoresponsive Colloids Drives Re‐Entrant Plasmon Coupling
summary: Plasmonic nanoparticles (NPs) integrated within thermoresponsive polymeric microgels provide a versatile platform for the realization of stimuli-responsive optical materials, where the microgel volume phase transition enables dynamic contro
content: Plasmonic nanoparticles (NPs) integrated within thermoresponsive polymeric microgels provide a versatile platform for the realization of stimuli-responsive optical materials, where the microgel volume phase transition enables dynamic control of plasmon coupling. This study uncovers a counter-intuitive re-entrant behavior with increasing NP loading in which plasmon coupling initially strengthens and subsequently weakens beyond a critical NP-to-microgel number ratio. By combining light and X-ray scattering techniques with optical spectroscopy and electrophoretic mobility measurements, it is demonstrated that plasmon coupling is governed not only by the interparticle distance between NPs confined within individual microgels but also by the colloidal stability of the hybrid complexes. At intermediate NP loadings, surface charge inhomogeneities induced by NP adsorption promote the aggregation of microgel-NP complexes, resulting in enhanced plasmon coupling. In contrast, when the complexes remain colloidally stable, coupling is dictated solely by NP organization within the corona of individual microgels. A quantitative relationship between plasmon coupling and interparticle distance reveals two distinct coupling regimes. This behavior is rationalized through a phase diagram linking colloidal stability to optical response. These findings identify colloidal stability as a key parameter for designing soft plasmonic systems with programmable optical properties.

title: Termite mounds as fertility islands and their benefits for raised-field agriculture in the floodplain of the Bangweulu Basin, Zambia
summary: Termite mounds are conspicuous features in tropical savannas, where the role of termites as ecosystem engineers is widely acknowledged. Among the many impacts of termites on the environment, modifications of the physicochemical properties o
content: Termite mounds are conspicuous features in tropical savannas, where the role of termites as ecosystem engineers is widely acknowledged. Among the many impacts of termites on the environment, modifications of the physicochemical properties of the soil are prominent, to the point that termites have influenced the agricultural and cultural practices of local communities. However, most studies have focused on dry savannas. We investigated the role of termite mounds as fertility islands, and their role in subsistence agriculture, in one of the world’s most extensive floodplain savannas, the Bangweulu basin in Zambia. First, based on inspection of satellite images, we showed that termite savannas and areas of raised-field agriculture (the main type of subsistence agriculture in the region) covered respectively 14 % and 23 % of the studied surface area, and overlapped. Second, investigating more specifically the area near the village of Yongolo, we evidenced two superimposed patterns of spatial distribution of termite mounds, one involving large mounds (mean height 1.7 m) and one involving small mounds (mean height 0.6 m), both regularly spaced with an average inter-mound distance of 68 m and 8 m, respectively. The two types of mounds differed in their termite communities, the large ones each hosting one nest of Odontotermes , the small ones hosting mostly nests of Trinervitermes and Cubitermes . Both mound types had soil properties that differed from those of the basin soil, leading to an expected increase in soil fertility on mounds (higher contents of N, C, organic matter and clay). Woody plants, including trees, occurred only on large mounds. On small mounds, the epigeal structure of termite nests was higher where depth of flood water was higher, showing plasticity in nest construction in response to environmental constraints. Termite mounds were extensively used by local people, in particular as preferred plots for building raised fields for cassava cultivation. Raised fields on termite mounds were richer in nitrogen and clay, but had a thinner layer of dark soil, than those off termite mounds. The main benefits of building raised fields on termite mounds appeared to be a longer duration of the cultivation period (allowing cultivation during the inundation period) and increased soil fertility through weathering of termite nest structures. Termite mounds (as fertility islands) and raised fields (built by piling up topsoil) both result in nutrient concentration. In addition, both termite nests and raised fields are built taller where flooding is deeper. Thus, termites and humans rely on analogous strategies to mitigate constraints in seasonally flooded savannas, showing convergence in niche construction.

title: Collective ignition characteristics of micron-sized iron particle streams
summary: Iron exhibits significant potential as a carbon-free fuel, yet the collective ignition and combustion characteristics of the particle streams are poorly understood. This work experimentally investigates the ignition and combustion behaviors
content: Iron exhibits significant potential as a carbon-free fuel, yet the collective ignition and combustion characteristics of the particle streams are poorly understood. This work experimentally investigates the ignition and combustion behaviors of micron-sized sponge iron particle streams in a multi-element diffusion flat-flame burner with precise control of the ambient conditions. Key parameters, including the ignition delay and particle temperature evolution are analyzed under varying temperatures and oxygen fractions. The results show that increasing oxygen fraction notably promotes ignition and raises particle temperatures, a trend that contrasts with single-particle ignition behavior. A statistical criterion based on 10% of the peak luminous intensity is adopted to define ignition delay, effectively capturing the collective ignition dynamics of particle ensembles. Finally, the study clarifies the distinct ignition mechanisms of particle streams, which may provide quantitative benchmarks for the modeling and design of iron-based combustion systems.

title: Porous Nanotubular Array Cathode With Nanoengineered Triple‐Phase Boundaries Toward Local O 2 Permeation
summary: ABSTRACT Ultra‐low Pt ordered cathodes confront low activity and water flooding owing to inadequate triple‐phase‐boundaries (TPBs). We infiltrate perfluorosulfonic acid solution into PtZn@Pt skin porous nanotubular array (PNA) with a thickn
content: ABSTRACT Ultra‐low Pt ordered cathodes confront low activity and water flooding owing to inadequate triple‐phase‐boundaries (TPBs). We infiltrate perfluorosulfonic acid solution into PtZn@Pt skin porous nanotubular array (PNA) with a thickness of 290 ± 40 nm and 54.8 ± 0.5 µg Pt cm −2 , thus fully coating it with resin layer up to 3 nm to nanoengineer TPBs. The PNA cathode demonstrates an excellent power density of 12.55 W mg Pt −1 . Besides electrochemically active surface area of 23.2 m 2 g Pt −1 and mass activity of 0.68 A mg Pt −1 , TPBs enable 39.0% improvement in relative to Pt/C cathode. 19.9 ± 4.7 nm tubular interiors and 2.0 ± 0.6 nm pores in tubular wall are beneficial for O 2 Knudsen diffusion. Molecular dynamics simulations (MD) indicate that TPBs offer 2.8‐fold improvement in local O 2 permeation and weaken van der Waals, rendering the PNA cathode to perform at 1 A cm −2 for 60 h without flooding.

title: Detailed-chemistry numerical investigation of flame-holder geometry effects on radiative performance and flame anchoring in premixed hydrogen micro-combustors
summary: Abstract Hydrogen-fueled micro-combustion systems are promising heat sources for micro-thermophotovoltaic (micro-TPV) applications, where improving radiative efficiency directly enhances electrical power output. This study numerically inves
content: Abstract Hydrogen-fueled micro-combustion systems are promising heat sources for micro-thermophotovoltaic (micro-TPV) applications, where improving radiative efficiency directly enhances electrical power output. This study numerically investigates premixed hydrogen–air combustion in a heated microchannel combustor using the full Yetter H2/O2 detailed kinetic mechanism (9 species, 21 elementary reactions) with In-Situ Adaptive Tabulation (ISAT), within a transient 2D finite-volume framework validated against published DNS data. The principal contribution is a systematic comparison of three equal-blockage bluff-body cross-sections (square, triangular, and semicircular) with explicit resolution of OH, H, and O radical distributions, conjugate heat transfer, and wall radiation. Parametric evaluations show that increasing the equivalence ratio toward stoichiometric conditions improves radiative efficiency up to 49.5%, whereas increasing inlet velocity from 10 to 30 m/s reduces efficiency from 28.82% to 5.07% due to residence-time constraints. At reference conditions (φ = 0.5, Uin = 10 m/s), the square flame holder achieves the highest radiative efficiency (30.46%), outperforming triangular and semicircular shapes up to 1.64 percentage points. Although inter-geometry differences are modest and close to grid sensitivity, the square geometry establishes a larger and stronger recirculation zone that promotes flame anchoring and wall thermal uniformity. These findings provide chemically detailed design insights for micro-TPV systems within acknowledged 2D and inert-wall modeling assumptions.

title: Recent thermohaline shifts in the Adriatic Sea and their potential consequences
summary: The Adriatic Sea has warmed and salinified rapidly over the past two decades, and the changes are not uniform with depth. We combine 33 664 quality-controlled shipboard and Argo temperature and salinity casts from 1950–2025 into two climato
content: The Adriatic Sea has warmed and salinified rapidly over the past two decades, and the changes are not uniform with depth. We combine 33 664 quality-controlled shipboard and Argo temperature and salinity casts from 1950–2025 into two climatologies, test the individual casts for regime shifts, and use the Argo profiles from the Southern Adriatic Pit to quantify the vertical structure of the changes. Between the 1950–1999 and 2000–2025 climatologies the southern Adriatic salinified at every depth and season, by 0.11–0.53, and warmed by up to 1.6 °C everywhere except at the uppermost levels in summer and autumn, where the sampling differs between the two periods. Amplification relative to the rest of the Mediterranean is strongly depth-dependent: below 700 m the southern Adriatic warms at 6.2 times the median rate of the other Mediterranean sub-basins, whereas above 200 m its warming is not amplified. The occurrence of near-surface salinity maxima (“surface saline lakes”) rises abruptly after 2014, in both ship and float records, from a few per cent of warm-season casts to about 40 %; this regime shift is only provable if vertical resolution and platform are accounted for. The intermediate salinity maximum has lost its dominant band: the detected maxima no longer cluster in one depth interval. Where two maxima coexist they have moved apart and diverged in density, so they are not one migrating core. Over 2014–2024 the steric contribution in the Southern Adriatic Pit is negative, dominated by halosteric contraction, so that local sea level rise must be mass-driven. Salt fingering has intensified below the classical intermediate core, allowing salt transport towards deeper layers. Three consequences follow, set out here as hypotheses. First, deep ventilation may persist under milder winters, because water that is already saline needs less cooling to sink, but each ventilation event may then deliver less oxygen, because the water that sinks is warmer. Second, exchange of oxygen, nutrients and carbon between the surface and intermediate layers may be either suppressed or enhanced beneath more frequent surface saline lakes, depending on whether stratification or double diffusion prevails. Third, Adriatic ecosystems, in which warming-linked mortality and species redistribution are already documented, face a basin changing faster at depth than at the surface. Testing these hypotheses requires sustained high-resolution observations.

title: Study on multi-objective water resources optimal allocation in water network areas based on water-energy-carbon synergistic governance
summary: Study area Northern Jiangsu Study focus Water resources optimal allocation is essential for coordinating regional water-use conflicts and promoting sustainable development. However, existing models face challenges in representing complex hy
content: Study area Northern Jiangsu Study focus Water resources optimal allocation is essential for coordinating regional water-use conflicts and promoting sustainable development. However, existing models face challenges in representing complex hydrodynamic processes in plain river networks with strong human interventions, and the integration of carbon considerations into water allocation remains limited. This study develops a Water-Economic-Carbon-Spatial Multi-objective Optimization Model (WEC-SMOM). The framework integrates generalized river network hydrodynamic modeling with NSGA-III-based multi-objective optimization and a projection pursuit-based compromise solution selection method to coordinate water-supply reliability, economic benefits, and carbon emissions under complex flow conditions. New hydrological insights for the region Applied to Northern Jiangsu, the proposed framework quantifies trade-offs among economic benefits, water-supply reliability, and carbon emissions. Results reveal two independent pathways for reducing water shortages. Under unchanged infrastructure conditions, the regional water shortage rate decreased from 2022 to 2035 by 4.4, 0.3, and 0.2 %age points under the 95%, 75%, and 50% water-supply guarantee scenarios, respectively. Under identical demand-year and hydrological conditions, HRSC-II reduces water shortages by an additional 2.7–5.4 %age points during extremely dry years compared with the pre-project scenario, with reductions exceeding 6 %age points in some terminal cities. These findings distinguish the contributions of demand management and infrastructure development and provide insights for sustainable allocation in complex river network systems.

title: Growing-season variability and environmental controls of CH 4 and N 2 O fluxes across high-latitude terrestrial ecosystems
summary: Rapid warming and accelerating ecological change across high-latitude (>66° N) terrestrial environments are reshaping greenhouse gas dynamics. However, spatiotemporal patterns and environmental drivers of CH 4 and N 2 O fluxes in high-latit
content: Rapid warming and accelerating ecological change across high-latitude (>66° N) terrestrial environments are reshaping greenhouse gas dynamics. However, spatiotemporal patterns and environmental drivers of CH 4 and N 2 O fluxes in high-latitude ecosystems remain poorly understood. In this study we describe the seasonal and spatial variation in CH 4 and N 2 O fluxes across key subarctic and boreal environmental gradients. A secondary aim is to examine the environmental drivers underlying these flux patterns. We measured fluxes during the snow-free season of 2024 and 2025 in northern Finland, starting early June (spring snowmelt) and ending late September (first snowfall). We conducted 1272 chamber measurements at 144 locations spanning eight high-latitude land cover classes: bare tundra, dwarf-shrub tundra, deciduous forest, evergreen forest, fen, bog, permafrost bog and tundra wetland. Bare tundra, dwarf-shrub tundra, deciduous forest and evergreen forest sites acted as net CH 4 sinks (mean flux of −0.16 to −0.05 mgm-2h-1, depending on land cover class) and as both N 2 O sources and sinks (−0.69 to 1.69 µgm-2h-1). Fen, bog, permafrost bog and tundra wetland sites were net CH 4 sources (mean flux of 0.93 to 27.81 mgm-2h-1) and net N 2 O sinks (−0.89 to −6.53 µgm-2h-1). Highest mean CH 4 fluxes occurred in fens (23.4 mgm-2h-1) and permafrost bogs (27.8 mgm-2h-1) which often coincided with substantial N 2 O sinks (mean flux of −6.53 in fens and −5.40 µgm-2h-1 in permafrost bogs). Seasonal trends were present for CH 4 but were land cover-dependent, with both sinks and sources typically peaking during July–August. Land cover class, soil temperature, and soil pH had the strongest effects on CH 4 fluxes while variation in N 2 O was best explained by soil pH and land cover class. However, a significant portion of the variability in N 2 O remained unexplained. These results demonstrate that strong spatial heterogeneity and pronounced seasonal dynamics during the snow-free period generate substantial variability in CH 4 and N 2 O fluxes across high-latitude ecosystems. Our findings suggest that monthly measurements of insitu gas fluxes and soil conditions in combination with accurate land cover mapping are essential for modelling and upscaling of GHG fluxes. This is especially important in high-latitude regions, where rapid warming is altering both ecosystem distributions and soil conditions with significant consequences for current and future GHG budgets.

title: Ultrasonic cryoporometry: determining pore-size distributions from acoustic measurements
summary: Abstract The standard experimental approaches for determining pore size distribution (PSD) are gas adsorption (e.g., nitrogen porosimetry) and mercury intrusion porosimetry. While widely used, these methods have limitations: gas adsorption
content: Abstract The standard experimental approaches for determining pore size distribution (PSD) are gas adsorption (e.g., nitrogen porosimetry) and mercury intrusion porosimetry. While widely used, these methods have limitations: gas adsorption experiments often require high-temperature heating and are less sensitive in macropores, whereas mercury intrusion is destructive and involves hazardous materials. Therefore, there is always a demand for alternative methods for characterization of porous materials. Thermodynamics of fluids confined in nanopores depend on the pore size. In particular, both the capillary condensation pressure and the freezing/melting point are shifted relative to their bulk values due to confinement. Capillary condensation is the basis of gas adsorption porosimetry, while the melting/freezing temperature shift can also be used for PSD determination through the Gibbs—Thomson equation, which links the transition temperature to the pore radius. This is the main idea of thermoporometric methods such as differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) based thermoporometry, and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) cryoporometry. Both techniques, however, typically require complex and costly instrumentation. Ultrasonic measurements provide an alternative route to probe phase transitions in porous materials. In ultrasonic pulse-transmission technique, speed of an ultrasonic wave depends on the density and elastic moduli of the composite system. When a fluid confined within nanopores freezes, the shear modulus of the composite increases, and the difference between the liquid-like and solid-like states reflects the contribution of the confined phase to the overall modulus. In this work, we analyze literature ultrasonic data for fluids (heptane, nonane, argon) confined in nanoporous media using a phenomenological model by Denoyel and Pellenq for phase transitions under confinement. We demonstrate that the temperature-dependent ultrasonic response provides information on the fraction of solidified fluid and, consequently, used to extract the pore size distribution. Our results suggest that ultrasonic data on porous materials can be used for determining PSD, providing an alternative to the methods based on NMR or DSC.

title: From Young to Older Disks: JWST/MIRI Evidence for Fading Molecular Emission and Hints for Elevated C/O in Upper Scorpius
summary: Abstract We present JWST/MIRI spectroscopy of 14 disks in the older (∼5–10 Myr) Upper Scorpius (USco) association and use slab of gas in local thermal equilibrium to infer basic gas properties. We find that one-half of these disks are molec
content: Abstract We present JWST/MIRI spectroscopy of 14 disks in the older (∼5–10 Myr) Upper Scorpius (USco) association and use slab of gas in local thermal equilibrium to infer basic gas properties. We find that one-half of these disks are molecular rich, with detections of H 2 O, CO 2 , HCN, C 2 H 2 , and H 2 , while the other one-half are molecular poor, showing no molecular emission other than H 2 . We further combine this sample with 10 other USco disks from the AGE-PRO program and compare the combined older sample to young (∼1–3 Myr) JDISCS Cycle 1 systems, which are analyzed in a similar manner. We find that USco disks have lower detection rates of major molecular species but a significantly higher detection rate of rarer C-bearing molecules such as C 4 H 2 .
